t: Severe Dysphagia Management Policy
This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to. Its aim is that each participant who
x: This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to. Its aim is that each participant who requires severe dysphagia management eats and drinks as safely, and as enjoyably, as their health allows. It is for participants, their families and advocates, our workers, and the people who check our work.

t: Everyone who works for [Provider name]: employees, contractors, agency workers, volunteers
x: Everyone who works for [Provider name]: employees, contractors, agency workers, volunteers and key personnel. Every support where we prepare, serve or help with a participant's food or drink. This includes their home, a shared home, a day program, respite and the community. Every participant whose swallowing difficulty is severe, or is suspected to be severe, until a speech pathologist says otherwise in writing. Severe dysphagia management sits on top of mealtime management. POL-MTM-01 Mealtime Management Policy applies to the same participant. POL-HID-03 Enteral Feeding and Management Policy applies where the participant is also tube fed. POL-HID-01 High Intensity Daily Personal Activities Policy sets the commitments shared by every high intensity support.

t: Commitments
We will identify every participant who requires severe dysphagia management. We screen eac
x: We will identify every participant who requires severe dysphagia management. We screen each participant for swallowing risk before their first meal with us. We screen again at every support plan review, and within 1 business day of any warning sign. A speech pathologist states in writing whether the participant requires it. We record the decision and keep one list of these participants.

t: We will treat a participant as requiring severe dysphagia management from the moment we su
x: We will treat a participant as requiring severe dysphagia management from the moment we suspect it, until a speech pathologist says otherwise in writing. We get written interim precautions from the participant's doctor or speech pathologist before the next meal. No worker or manager chooses a texture, a drink thickness or a food restriction.

t: We will ask a speech pathologist with expertise in severe dysphagia management to assess s
x: We will ask a speech pathologist with expertise in severe dysphagia management to assess swallowing, with the participant's consent. We also ask them to write or endorse the plan. We ask within 2 business days of consent, and on the same day when a sign is urgent. We ask other practitioners when the speech pathologist or the screen advises.

t: We will ask the speech pathologist to review the assessment and the plan at least every 12
x: We will ask the speech pathologist to review the assessment and the plan at least every 12 months, or by the earlier date they set. We also ask for a review within 1 business day of any change or difficulty a worker sees. Examples are choking, coughing that stops a meal, a chest infection, a hospital stay, an unplanned weight change, a new medicine that the pharmacist or prescriber says may affect swallowing or alertness, and a change in alertness. Other medicine changes go to the pharmacist first.

t: We will involve each participant in their assessment and their plan, in their usual way of
x: We will involve each participant in their assessment and their plan, in their usual way of communicating, and record their consent. We respect and record an informed choice to eat or drink differently from the plan. We never withdraw support because of that choice.

t: We will support each participant under one written plan that a speech pathologist wrote or
x: We will support each participant under one written plan that a speech pathologist wrote or endorsed. It states their needs and preferences: food and drink levels, preparation and testing, equipment, position, pace, supervision, mouth care, medicines, and what they like. We do not use a plan until a practitioner has answered each of those points.

t: We will make sure each plan sets out how risks, incidents and emergencies are managed for
x: We will make sure each plan sets out how risks, incidents and emergencies are managed for that participant. It names the signs to watch for and what the worker does for each. It says when to call 000, who to phone and how fast. It also says what happens before the next meal after an event.

t: We will train each worker for each participant before they support a meal. A speech pathol
x: We will train each worker for each participant before they support a meal. A speech pathologist with expertise in severe dysphagia management gives the training and signs the worker off. Where the speech pathologist nominates them, another appropriately qualified health practitioner with documented expertise in severe dysphagia management may train and sign off instead. The training covers the participant's needs, how to manage a severe dysphagia incident, and the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor. A sign-off lapses after 3 months without supporting the participant, and when the clinical content of the plan changes (a new review date or phone number does not lapse it). We train and sign off again when it lapses, and every 12 months. We roster only signed-off workers to a meal.

t: We will support every meal, snack and drink round the same way. The worker reads the plan
x: We will support every meal, snack and drink round the same way. The worker reads the plan and prepares to the stated levels. They test, position the participant, help at the set pace and watch for signs. They keep the participant upright afterwards and record the meal on the same day.

t: We will respond to every choking event, and every sign that food or drink went into the lu
x: We will respond to every choking event, and every sign that food or drink went into the lungs. The response is first aid, a 000 call where needed, an incident report, and a medical review the same day after choking that needed first aid and after any sign that food or drink went into the lungs: a wet or gurgly voice, a change of colour, shortness of breath, or chest signs in the hours or days after a meal. We tell the speech pathologist the same day. We give nothing more by mouth except as the participant's plan allows while advice is sought. We follow our incident procedures. We notify the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days.

t: We will keep the current plan at every place the participant eats or drinks, where a worke
x: We will keep the current plan at every place the participant eats or drinks, where a worker can find it in under a minute. We remove older versions the same day. With consent, we send the plan with the participant to hospital and to other services. We treat discharge instructions as interim precautions.

x: We will check each participant's meal records every week for completeness, and the Clinical Lead will read a sample of each participant's records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change, and act on what they show. We report trends in choking and swallowing incidents to the governing body every 3 months.

t: severe dysphagia: difficulty swallowing, chewing or biting that a speech pathologist or do
x: severe dysphagia: difficulty swallowing, chewing or biting that a speech pathologist or doctor says puts the participant at serious risk. The risks are choking, food or drink going into the lungs, poor nutrition and dehydration. severe dysphagia management: the support a participant with severe dysphagia needs to eat and drink safely. It includes the plan, trained workers, support at every meal and the response to choking. plan: the participant's Mealtime Management Plan (FRM-MTM-01), written or endorsed by a speech pathologist, with the extra points PRO-HID-03 requires for severe dysphagia. speech pathologist: a health practitioner who assesses swallowing and holds the credential of their professional body. Where this policy says a speech pathologist trains or signs off a worker, it also means another appropriately qualified health practitioner with documented expertise in severe dysphagia management whom the speech pathologist nominates. expertise in severe dysphagia management: regular clinical work with people who have severe dysphagia. The practitioner shows it in a written statement of how long, where and with whom, kept in REG-HID-02. signed off: a speech pathologist has watched the worker carry out this participant's plan correctly, and the worker has signed that they can follow it. A sign-off covers one participant. It lapses after 3 months without supporting the participant, and when the clinical content of the plan changes; a new review date or phone number does not lapse it. interim precautions: written advice from the participant's doctor or speech pathologist about meals until the plan is in place. drink round: any drink offered between meals. Every drink round is supported and recorded the same way as a meal. aspiration: food, drink or saliva going into the lungs. It can happen without a cough. IDDSI: the International Dysphagia Diet Standardisation Initiative framework. It names food textures and drink thicknesses by number. informed choice: a decision the participant makes after the risks and options are explained in a way they understand. Clinical Lead: a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Control
Severe Dysphagia Management Procedure
The result: every participant who requires severe dysphagia management is found and assess
x: The result: every participant who requires severe dysphagia management is found and assessed by a speech pathologist. Trained workers support them at every meal, under one written plan made with them. Choking, and food or drink going into the lungs, get the right response straight away. This procedure gives effect to POL-HID-04 Severe Dysphagia Management Policy, C1 to C12. It sits on top of PRO-MTM-01 Mealtime Management Procedure. Both apply to this participant. There is one plan at the table: FRM-MTM-01 Mealtime Management Plan, with the extra points in Decision table 2. Where a Record line names a form or register that is not yet a Rise template, record the same facts in the participant's file under the same heading until it is.

t: Start this procedure: when the mealtime screen (FRM-MTM-02 Nutrition and Swallowing Risk S
x: Start this procedure: when the mealtime screen (FRM-MTM-02 Nutrition and Swallowing Risk Screen) or a practitioner's report shows that severe dysphagia is known or suspected, from step 1 at every support plan review and after any warning sign, from step 1 at every meal, snack and drink round for a participant who requires severe dysphagia management, from step 13. Severe dysphagia is difficulty swallowing, chewing or biting that a speech pathologist or doctor says puts the participant at serious risk. The risks are choking, food or drink going into the lungs, poor nutrition and dehydration. We never decide how severe it is ourselves. Who acts: The Clinical Lead decides and records who requires severe dysphagia management. They arrange assessment, the plan check, training and reviews. They read a sample of each participant's meal records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change. The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. The speech pathologist assesses swallowing and writes or endorses the plan. They train workers and sign them off, or nominate another appropriately qualified health practitioner with documented expertise in severe dysphagia management to do so. They must have expertise in severe dysphagia management. Other practitioners add to the plan: a dietitian, an occupational therapist, a physiotherapist, the participant's doctor, a pharmacist and a dentist. The Service Manager takes the participant's consent, rosters signed-off workers, keeps REG-HID-01 and REG-HID-02, checks every shift's meal records for completeness each week, puts the plan in place and sends it with the participant. The worker at the meal prepares, tests, helps, watches and records. The on-call manager takes calls at any meal. In office hours this is the Service Manager. After hours it is the rostered manager. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether an event is a reportable incident and notifies the NDIS Commission. In a small provider one person may hold several of these roles. A sole trader is the Service Manager and the worker at the meal. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. A sole trader cannot sign off their own competency; the speech pathologist does that. Before you take on the participant, a named second person, another provider's worker or a supporter the plan names, must be trained and signed off by the speech pathologist and on the sign-off list, so that a sole trader who is ill leaves a signed-off person to cover the meal. Where a step says to phone a manager, a sole trader writes down the time and phones the Clinical Lead, the speech pathologist or the participant's doctor directly. A concern about a sole trader goes to the independent contact for concerns named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register.

You know where the participant's plan is kept. You know the on-call number: [on-call number]. You have the thickener, the equipment and the test tools the plan names. Clinical Lead: You can open REG-HID-02 High Intensity Supports Register and REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register. t: Choking can kill within minutes. If the participant cannot cough, speak or breathe, call 0
x: Choking can kill within minutes. If the participant cannot cough, speak or breathe, call 000 before you call a manager. No cough does not mean safe. Food and drink can go into the lungs without a cough. The harm shows hours or days later as a chest infection. Follow the plan even when the participant seems fine. Never choose or change a texture, a thickness, a position or the plan. Only the speech pathologist does. The wrong level can block the airway or put food or drink into the lungs. A drowsy participant cannot protect their airway. Food, drink or a medicine given by mouth to a drowsy person can go into the lungs. Texture changes as food cools, stands or is reheated. A meal that passed the test an hour ago can fail now. Some foods hide thin liquid. Ice cream, jelly, juicy fruit and soup with pieces turn to thin liquid in the mouth. The plan lists what to avoid. A crushed or mixed medicine can harm. Only the prescriber or a pharmacist can say a medicine may be altered, in writing. Dry thickener powder is a choking hazard. Store it where the plan says. A worker who is not signed off must not help at a meal. They do not know this participant's needs or the choking response. Force is never used. Forcing food, or holding a person to feed them, is abuse.

t: Get written interim precautions from the participant's doctor or speech pathologist.
x: Get written interim precautions from the participant's doctor or speech pathologist. A texture or thickness chosen by a worker or a manager can cause choking, or put food or drink into the lungs. severe dysphagia is required or suspected, and no plan is in place The Clinical Lead Phone the practitioner, with the participant if they agree. Write their name, profession, the date and time, and their advice. Read each food and drink level back to them by its IDDSI number and name, and each other precaution in full, and wait for them to confirm. Ask them to send written confirmation (a secure message or email from the practice counts as written) before the next business day; until it arrives, workers follow the advice as read back. t: Control
Tracheostomy Management Procedure
The result: each participant with a tracheostomy has a plan made with them by a qualified
x: The result: each participant with a tracheostomy has a plan made with them by a qualified health practitioner. Every worker who cares for them is trained for them and signed off. Care follows the plan every shift. An airway emergency meets a rehearsed response. This procedure gives effect to POL-HID-05 Tracheostomy Management Policy, C1 to C14. In this procedure: the plan: the participant's tracheostomy plan, written by their practitioner and held with FRM-HID-01 Participant Health Support Plan. the skills descriptor: the NDIS Commission's High Intensity Support Skills Descriptor for tracheostomy support. the Incident Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018. the Restrictive Practices Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Start at step 1 when a participant with a tracheostomy asks us for support. Start there to
x: Start at step 1 when a participant with a tracheostomy asks us for support. Start there too when a participant we already support has a tracheostomy placed. After a new tracheostomy or a tube change, care by our workers starts or restarts only from the date the practitioner writes in the plan, with any extra rule the practitioner sets for that period. Steps 10 to 20 run every shift. Steps 21 to 26 run the moment an airway emergency starts. Steps 27 to 30 run after an event, at each review, every week and every month. A tracheostomy is an opening in the neck, called a stoma, that holds a tube so the participant can breathe. An airway emergency is any event in which the participant cannot get enough air through the tube, the stoma, the mouth or the nose. Decision table 2 lists the signs. Who acts: The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers tracheostomy care, whom we engage to oversee this support. They arrange the practitioner's assessment and check the plan. They set the training plan, review incidents, book reviews, read a sample of the care record every month, and read every record after an incident or a plan change. The participant's health practitioner assesses the participant, writes and reviews the plan, and decides every clinical value in it. This is a medical practitioner, nurse practitioner, registered nurse or other health practitioner whose training and scope cover tracheostomy care. They are the participant's own, not our employee. The trainer trains each worker and signs off each task. This is the practitioner, or a person who meets the skills descriptor for tracheostomy support. The Clinical Lead checks their qualification first. The Service Manager asks for the participant's consent, rosters signed-off workers, puts the plan where workers can reach it, and checks every care record for completeness each week. In office hours the Service Manager is also the on-call manager. The worker on shift cares for the participant under the plan. A signed-off worker has a sign-off for this participant in REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register. It lists the tasks they may do, and it covers one participant only. The on-call manager takes workers' calls at any hour: the Service Manager in office hours, the rostered manager after hours. A clinical question goes to the practitioner, or to the Clinical Lead. The authorised notifier, who is the Quality Manager, decides whether an incident is reportable. In a small provider one person may hold several of these roles. A sole trader is the Service Manager, the on-call manager and the worker on shift. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead or trainer, and cannot sign off their own competency. They engage a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers tracheostomy care, for both. Three tasks are never done by the sole trader alone: the plan check at step 4, which the engaged Clinical Lead does with the participant's practitioner; the sign-off at step 7, which the practitioner or another trainer does; and the clinical review at step 28, which a person outside the business does. A sole trader who is the only signed-off worker has no cover. They need a second signed-off person for the tasks that need two, and for leave, and name that person at Q77 before taking on the participant. Where a step says to phone the on-call manager, a sole trader phones the practitioner and writes down the time. A sole trader checks their own record for completeness each week and sends a copy to the engaged Clinical Lead every month, who does the sample read at step 30 (our standard).

t: Call 000 first in an airway emergency. A blocked or displaced tube can stop breathing with
x: Call 000 first in an airway emergency. A blocked or displaced tube can stop breathing within minutes. A call to the practitioner or a manager first costs time the participant does not have. Never force a catheter or a tube. Force can tear the airway or push a blockage deeper. Suction takes air as well as secretions. Suction that is too long, too deep or too hard can drop the participant's oxygen and injure the airway. Use only the limits in the plan. Never change the ties alone. One person changing ties can let the tube come out. The practitioner changes them with you as the second person, or two signed-off workers the plan names change them together. Nobody changes them alone. A valve or cap on a tube with an inflated cuff can stop breathing out. Fit one only as the plan says. Water or loose material near the stoma can be breathed in. A shower, a bath, a bib, powder or fluff can block the airway, cause an infection or drown the participant. Follow the plan's rules for water and for covering the stoma. Do only what you are signed off for. A task done without a sign-off can harm the participant. It can also breach the Code of Conduct duty to give safe and competent support. Never guess a value. A value from memory, or from another participant's plan, can be wrong for this participant. Read Section A. A change in secretions, a new smell or any blood can be the first sign of trouble. Report it straight away, during the shift. Waiting until the end of the shift can cost the participant their airway. Never restrain a participant to give care. Force can harm them, and a hold or device used to stop their movement may be a restrictive practice.

t: Steps
Ask the participant to agree to a health practitioner's assessment, to health reviews and
x: Ask the participant to agree to a health practitioner's assessment, to health reviews and to sharing their plan. The Service Manager Use the participant's own way of communicating (FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form). Offer an independent advocate and a supporter of their choice. A decision maker agrees only within the authority they hold. Explain what each yes or no means. Say who we would share the plan with, and why. If the participant says no to the assessment, explain that we cannot start tracheostomy care without a practitioner's plan. Offer to help them find one. If they say no to reviews or to sharing, explain the risk, offer an advocate, write their words and respect the choice. Never pressure the participant. The participant has chosen, knowing what each choice means, and their choice is on record. FRM-HID-08 Q7; FRM-INF-01 Before any tracheostomy support starts (our standard)

The practitioner must be qualified in tracheostomy care. Send them Section A of FRM-HID-08 to use as the summary page of the plan. A named, qualified practitioner is booked to assess the participant, and the participant knows when. FRM-HID-08 Q4; REG-HID-02 Before any tracheostomy support starts (our standard)

t: Assess the participant and write the plan with them.

t: Set the training plan for this participant.
x: Set the training plan for this participant. The Clinical Lead List every worker who will support the participant, and set what each needs. t: Train each worker on this participant's tube, equipment and emergency pages.
x: Train each worker on this participant's tube, equipment and emergency pages. The trainer Train in the participant's home, on their own equipment, as the participant agrees. t: Watch each worker do each task, and sign off the tasks they do safely.

t: Take the observations the plan asks for.
x: Take the observations the plan asks for. The worker on shift Take only the observations at Q24, with the equipment the plan names. Look and listen first: breathing, colour and alertness. Then take each value. Write each value with its unit and the time. Never estimate a value, and never take one the plan does not ask for. Compare each value with the participant's own limits at Q25. A value outside the limits goes to step 19 or step 21, as the lists at Q27 and Q28 say. The record shows how the participant was breathing and what their readings were, and whether any is outside their limits. FRM-HID-08 Q50 to Q52 As often as the plan sets at Q24 (the participant's plan)

t: Look at the tube, the ties and the stoma without touching the tube.
x: Look at the tube, the ties and the stoma without touching the tube. Pulling or adjusting the tube can pull it out or injure the airway. The worker on shift Check the tube sits as it did last shift. Check the ties are in place, clean and dry. Look at the pilot balloon and write whether the cuff appears inflated or deflated, and whether a valve or cap is on, as Q11 and Q12 say. Measuring the cuff pressure, or inflating or deflating the cuff, is a different task (Decision table 1). Look at the skin round the stoma for redness, swelling, wetness, smell, discharge, sore skin or bleeding. Write what you see. A tube that has moved, loose ties or a new sign of infection goes to step 19 straight away. A tube that is out or partly out is an emergency: go to step 23. Any change in the tube, the ties or the skin is seen and written down. FRM-HID-08 Q53 and Q54 At the start of every shift, and at each care task (our standard)

t: Suction the participant as the plan sets.
x: Suction the participant as the plan sets. Suction takes air as well as secretions. Suction that is too long, too deep or too hard can drop the participant's oxygen and injure the airway. The participant shows a sign at Q16, or asks for suction A worker signed off for suction Wash your hands and put on the protection the plan names. Tell the participant what you are about to do. Position them as the plan says, and move the head and neck only as the plan says. Use the catheter, the pressure, the depth, the time and the technique at Q17. Use only the catheter the plan names. Never wet it from a basin or an open container. Never put water or saline into the tube unless the plan says to. Stop straight away at a stop sign at Q18. Stop too if the participant's colour changes, they are distressed or the catheter will not pass. Never force it, and go to step 21. Check breathing and colour after each episode. Suction by the clock only where the plan sets a time. The airway is clear, or you have stopped and called for help. The record shows each episode. FRM-HID-08 Q55 to Q60 When a sign appears or the participant asks, within the limits at Q17 (the participant's plan)

t: Give the daily care the plan sets.
x: Give the daily care the plan sets. The worker on shift Do only the care the plan gives you at Q19 to Q23. This can include cleaning the stoma and the skin, mouth care, humidification and washing. Inner cannula care, measuring or changing the cuff, deflating the cuff before a valve or cap and reinflating it after, and fitting a speaking valve or cap are different. A worker does them only when the plan names them at Q37 for that task and their sign-off lists it. A worker who is not signed off for the cuff step never fits a valve or cap on a cuffed tube. The rest of the tube care stays with the practitioner. Keep water away from the tube at every wash, and keep the stoma covered as the plan says. Watch for coughing or a wet voice after eating or drinking. Oxygen is a prescribed medicine: give it, or a nebulised treatment, only as the plan sets and at the flow it prescribes, and sign it on FRM-MED-01. Write what you did and what you found, including the humidification care (Q61). The participant has had the care the plan sets, and the record shows each task and what you found. FRM-HID-08 Q61 to Q63, Q65 and Q66 At the times the plan sets at Q21 and Q19 (the participant's plan)

t: Help the practitioner change the ties or the dressing as the second person, or change them
x: Help the practitioner change the ties or the dressing as the second person, or change them with the other named worker where the plan names you both. Ties changed by one person can let the tube come out. A tie or dressing change is due, or the ties are loose, wet or soiled A worker signed off to assist, or two signed-off workers the plan names at Q37 to change the ties together The practitioner changes the ties, as the skills descriptor sets, with you as the second person: you steady the tube and the participant's head as they direct, and pass what they ask for. Where the practitioner's plan names two signed-off workers to change the ties together (Q14 and Q37), and the law of [state or territory] allows it, you change them as the plan sets, one steadying the tube and the other changing the ties. Never change the ties alone. Never cut the old ties before the new ones are secure. If the ties are loose, wet or soiled and nobody the plan names is there, do not change them. Hold the tube steady, keep the participant still and phone the practitioner at Q5. Follow their instruction and write their words. If the tube moves or comes out, go to step 23. The ties or the dressing have been changed by the people the plan names, never by one person alone, and the tube stayed in place. FRM-HID-08 Q64 When the change at Q14 is due, and straight away if the ties are loose (the participant's plan)

t: Clean the equipment and dispose of waste.
x: Clean the equipment and dispose of waste. The worker on shift Wash your hands, then put on gloves. Put used catheters, gloves and dressings in the bag the plan names, and close it. Dispose of clinical waste as PRO-WST-01 Management of Waste Procedure sets. Clean or change the suction canister and tubing, and any reusable part, as the plan and the maker's instructions say. Use standard precautions every time. Put back any kit item you used. Tell the Service Manager of any supply at its minimum stock. The equipment is clean and ready, the waste is out of the home and the kit is complete. FRM-HID-08 Q67 Straight after each care task, and before your shift ends (our standard)

t: Phone the practitioner and tell them what you found.
x: Phone the practitioner and tell them what you found. A small change can be the start of a blockage or an infection. Waiting until the end of the shift can cost the participant their airway. A value is outside the limits at Q25, secretions have changed, there is any blood, or anything on the list at Q28 has happened The worker on shift Use the number at Q5. Say who the participant is, what you saw or measured and when, what you have done and how they are now. Write down the practitioner's words and their instruction, and follow it. Use Decision table 3 to see whom else to tell. If you cannot reach the practitioner after trying twice in 10 minutes, use the after-hours number, then phone the on-call manager. Call 000 if the participant looks worse. The practitioner knows, and has told you what to do. FRM-HID-08 Q69 Straight away (our standard)

t: Finish the record and hand over to the next worker.
x: Finish the record and hand over to the next worker. The worker on shift Check that every question for your shift has an answer. Write values, not ticks. Sign with your initials and the time. Tell the next worker what you found, did and reported, and what is still open. Leave the record where the next worker will see it. Put anything that is not about the tracheostomy in FRM-SUP-08 Progress Note and Shift Handover Record. If you or the participant think the plan is not meeting their needs, write it at Q72. The next worker starts with the full picture, and the record is complete. FRM-HID-08 Q72 and Q73 Before you leave the shift (our standard)

t: Call 000.
x: Call 000. A blocked or displaced tube can stop breathing within minutes. A call to the practitioner or a manager first costs time the participant does not have. The participant shows any sign in Decision table 2, or anything on the list at Q27, or you are unsure The worker on shift, or any person with the participant If a second person is there, tell them to call and to stay with you. Say: "This person has a tracheostomy." Then say what is happening, how the person breathes (Q9) and the address. Say if they have an advance care directive. Put the phone on speaker and follow the operator's words. Send someone to the door to meet the ambulance. Have the plan, the kit and any tube that came out ready for the crew. Go straight on to step 22, step 23, step 24, step 25 or step 26 while the operator stays on the line. An ambulance is coming and the participant is not alone. FRM-HID-08 Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Try to clear the tube with the blocked tube page of the plan.
x: Try to clear the tube with the blocked tube page of the plan. Never force a catheter into a blocked tube. Force can tear the airway or push the blockage deeper. The participant struggles to breathe, no air moves through the tube, their colour has changed, or the catheter will not pass The worker on shift Sit the participant up, or position them as the plan says. Take off anything on the end of the tube: a speaking valve, a cap, a heat and moisture exchanger or a ventilator connection. If the plan names you at Q37 for it, take out the inner cannula and put in a clean one. If you are signed off for suction, suction once as the plan sets, and stop if the catheter will not pass. If the plan names oxygen and you are signed off for it, give it to the face and the stoma. The plan's blocked tube page may then name two more tasks for a worker: deflating the cuff, and, where Q9 says air passes through the mouth and nose, removing a tube that cannot be cleared. Do them only if the plan names you at Q37 and your sign-off lists them, in the order the page sets and in the way it says. The practitioner sets that order and those words. Tell the 000 operator what you have done. Keep going until the crew arrives. If breathing stops, go to step 25. The tube is clear and the participant is breathing. Or the crew arrives and the participant has had every step on the page that you are signed off for. FRM-HID-08 Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Keep the airway open and stay with the participant until help comes.
x: Keep the airway open and stay with the participant until help comes. A tube that has come out can leave the participant unable to breathe. A tube pushed in the wrong way can injure the airway or close it. The tube is out or partly out The worker on shift If step 21 is not done, tell a second person to call 000 now. Keep the participant sitting up if they are awake, unless the plan says otherwise. Do not push the tube back in. The one exception is a worker the plan names at Q37 for putting in a spare tube, who is signed off. That worker uses the spare the plan names, and the smaller size if it will not go in. Stop at once if you meet any resistance. If you are not named, put nothing into the stoma. Then follow the branch for this participant at Q9. Q9 says YES, air passes through the mouth and nose: keep the participant calm, watch their breathing, and cover the stoma only if the plan's page says to. Q9 says NO, the participant breathes only through the neck: never cover the stoma, keep it clear, and give oxygen at the stoma if the plan has it and you are signed off. Q9 says PARTLY: follow the plan's page for this participant. If the participant stops breathing, go to step 25. Keep the tube that came out for the crew. The participant is breathing, or is supported until the crew arrives. A spare tube is put in only by a worker the plan names. FRM-HID-08 Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Stay with the participant, keep the airway open and act on where the blood comes from.
x: Stay with the participant, keep the airway open and act on where the blood comes from. Blood comes from the tube or stoma, or is in the secretions, and is more than the plan's streak or does not stop The worker on shift Call 000 first (step 21). Keep the participant upright if they are awake, unless the plan says otherwise. Blood from the skin at the edge of the stoma: press a clean pad gently on the skin beside the stoma, never over the tube opening or the stoma. Blood from inside the tube: press nothing; sit the participant up, keep the airway clear with suction only if you are signed off and the airway is filling, and tell the 000 operator that blood is coming from inside the tube. Never take the tube out. Keep any soaked pads, and tell the crew when the bleeding started. If the participant stops breathing, go to step 25. A streak of blood within the plan's limit goes to step 19. The airway stays open, bleeding at the skin is pressed, and help is coming. FRM-HID-08 Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Check for breathing, and start CPR if it is not normal.
x: Check for breathing, and start CPR if it is not normal. The participant does not respond, or is only gasping The worker on shift Check for a response and for breathing. If the participant does not respond but is breathing normally, do not start compressions. Place them in the recovery position as you were trained, keep the stoma clear and uncovered, and watch their breathing until the crew arrives. If they are not breathing, or only gasping, send for the defibrillator and start chest compressions straight away, as you were trained. Give breaths where the plan's resuscitation page says: through the tube, at the stoma, or at the mouth and nose with the stoma covered. Use the resuscitation bag in the kit as your CPR training for this participant covered. If your training does not cover CPR for a person with a tracheostomy, give chest compressions only, keep the stoma uncovered and follow the 000 operator. If the tube is blocked and you cannot clear it, the plan's resuscitation page says what to do with the breaths, and step 22 says which tasks a named worker may do. Use the defibrillator as the machine directs. Keep going until the crew takes over, the participant moves or breathes, or you cannot go on. Do not stop to look for the plan. Tell the crew about any advance care directive. If the plan holds a signed decision not to resuscitate, its page says what to do. If you have no such page, start CPR. The participant gets the right help without delay, CPR or the recovery position, until the crew takes over. FRM-HID-08 Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Switch to the backup in the plan.
x: Switch to the backup in the plan. The suction unit, the humidifier or other equipment fails, or the power goes out, while the participant needs it The worker on shift If suction fails, use the backup at Q36. If the humidifier fails, use the backup humidification the plan names. If the power goes, move to battery equipment and check each item is on. Phone the on-call manager. If no backup works and the participant needs suction or shows a sign in Decision table 2, call 000 (step 21). If the participant also uses a ventilator, follow PRO-HID-06 Ventilator Management Procedure as well. If the home must be left, follow FRM-SUP-07 Participant Emergency and Disaster Plan and take the kit and the plan. Keep the faulty item out of use until it is fixed, and tell the Service Manager the same day. The participant keeps the care they need, or help is coming. FRM-HID-08 Q48 and Q70 Straight away (our standard)

t: Report the event to the on-call manager, then write the incident report.
x: Report the event to the on-call manager, then write the incident report. The worker on shift Do this after any airway emergency, call to 000, tube out, error or near miss. Do it too after a blocked tube that needed more than the usual suction. Do it too after a worker is splashed or pricked by secretions or blood. For a splash or a prick, wash the area with soap and water and rinse the eyes with clean water, then seek medical assessment straight away, within hours and not at the end of the day. It is also a work health and safety incident. Phone the on-call manager as soon as the participant is safe. Complete the incident report form (FRM-INC-01) before your shift ends, and record the incident type as a health emergency. Write what you saw, did and said, in the order it happened. Say if the participant went to hospital. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether it is reportable under PRO-INC-02 Reportable Incidents Notification Procedure, and notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days. Tell the practitioner straight away, during the shift. Write the report number at Q71 and keep any used equipment. The on-call manager tells the Clinical Lead, and the people the participant chose are told as PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure sets. The on-call manager knows, PRO-INC-01 has started and the report number is on the record. FRM-INC-01 (incident type); FRM-HID-08 Q71 Phone as soon as the participant is safe (our standard). Write before your shift ends (our standard). A worker must tell a manager of a reportable incident as soon as possible (statutory: the Incident Rules, section 19)

t: Review the incident clinically, and ask the practitioner for their review.
x: Review the incident clinically, and ask the practitioner for their review. The Clinical Lead Read the incident report and the care record for the shifts before it. Ask what the participant's breathing, secretions and readings showed in the days before. Ask whether the plan, the equipment, the training or the roster played a part. Ask the practitioner to review the plan and the participant, and record the date you asked. Ask whether any worker needs to be assessed again (Decision table 4). PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure asks for the participant's own views. Write each action with an owner and a date in the incident assessment (FRM-INC-01). Support the worker. Reporting is never punished. The cause is understood, the plan is reviewed where it needs to be, and every action has an owner and a date. FRM-INC-01 (clinical review and actions); REG-HID-02 The Clinical Lead's review within 1 business day of the incident, and the same day when it needed 000. The practitioner's review is asked for within 1 business day (our standard)

t: Act on Decision table 4.
x: Act on Decision table 4. The Clinical Lead Check REG-HID-02 every week for review dates coming due. Book the practitioner's review at the interval at Q8, and whenever a row in Decision table 4 applies. Ask the participant what is working, what they want changed and whether they want an advocate there. Ask workers whether the plan is meeting the participant's needs (Q72). Send the practitioner the care record. After the review, the practitioner updates the plan. Then repeat step 4 for the changed answers and step 9 for the copies. Book worker assessments that a row calls for. Record the review and the date of the next one. The review or assessment is booked and held, the participant's views are recorded, and the plan and Section A match again. FRM-HID-08 Q8 and Q75; REG-HID-02 As Decision table 4 sets for each row (our standard)

t: Check the care record for completeness each week, and read a sample each month.
x: Check the care record for completeness each week, and read a sample each month. The Service Manager, then the Clinical Lead Service Manager, every week: check every shift's entries for answers left blank or written as ticks, missed kit checks, and tasks initialled by a worker whose sign-off does not list them. Phone the worker about each gap. Clinical Lead, every month: read a sample of the participant's records, and every record after an incident or a plan change. Look for readings outside the limits that nobody reported, and for changes in secretions or skin across the days. If the record shows a trend, ask the practitioner for a review. Send trends to the Quality Manager for the 3 month audit. Every gap in completeness is found within a week, every clinical trend within a month, and each has an action. FRM-HID-08 Q74 Every week for completeness. Every month for the sample, and after every incident or plan change (our standard)

t: Control
Ventilator management
x: Each participant requiring ventilator management receives appropriate support relevant and proportionate to their individual needs and the specific ventilator used.

t: Each participant is involved in the assessment and development of the plan for their venti
x: Each participant is involved in the assessment and development of the plan for their ventilator management. With their consent, the participant’s health status is subject to regular and timely review by an appropriately qualified health practitioner. The plan identifies how risks, incidents and emergencies will be managed, including required actions and escalation to ensure participant wellbeing.

t: Appropriate policies and procedures are in place, including a training plan for workers, t
x: Appropriate policies and procedures are in place, including a training plan for workers, that relate to the support provided to each participant who is ventilator dependent.

t: All workers have completed training, relating specifically to each participant’s ventilati
x: All workers have completed training, relating specifically to each participant’s ventilation needs, managing a related incident and the high intensity support skills descriptor for ventilator management, delivered by an appropriately qualified health practitioner or person who meets the high intensity support skills descriptor for ventilator management.

t: Ventilator Management Policy
This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to so that each participant who uses a v
x: This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to so that each participant who uses a ventilator gets safe support that fits them and their own machine. It is for participants, their families and advocates, our workers, and the people who check our work.

t: Everyone who works for [Provider name]: employees, contractors, agency workers, volunteers
x: Everyone who works for [Provider name]: employees, contractors, agency workers, volunteers and key personnel. Every participant for whom a worker starts, fits, checks, cleans or answers a ventilator. This includes a ventilator used through a mask and one used through a tracheostomy. It includes bilevel and CPAP machines where the treating team says the participant depends on the device or cannot manage it without a worker. Otherwise, help with a CPAP or bilevel machine is ordinary personal care under the participant's plan. Every setting: the participant's home, a shared home, a day program, a vehicle and the community. A ventilator that the participant sets up and uses entirely alone is outside this policy, unless their plan says workers must help.

t: Commitments
We will start ventilator support only under a written plan and prescription from the parti
x: We will start ventilator support only under a written plan and prescription from the participant's treating team. We start only after the readiness check in FRM-HID-10 is complete and signed. We never write, fill a gap in or change the plan.

t: We will make each plan with the participant, in their usual way of communicating. We recor
x: We will make each plan with the participant, in their usual way of communicating. We record how they took part, their choices, how they call for help by day and by night, and any advance care directive.

t: We will ask the treating team, with the participant's consent, to review their ventilator
x: We will ask the treating team, with the participant's consent, to review their ventilator support and health. We ask at the interval the team sets, and at least every 12 months. We ask within 1 business day of a trigger in PRO-HID-06 Decision table 8, and the same day when it is urgent.

t: We will check the ventilator display against the prescription at the start of every shift
x: We will check the ventilator display against the prescription at the start of every shift and after every restart. We check the circuit and the interface too, and record the result. A difference goes to the treating team before anything else. No worker or manager changes a setting or an alarm limit.

t: We will follow the staffing rule in PRO-HID-06 Decision table 1 on every shift. For a part
x: We will follow the staffing rule in PRO-HID-06 Decision table 1 on every shift. For a participant who cannot safely be off the ventilator, a signed-off worker is awake and within hearing of the alarm the whole time. A worker rostered alone holds current CPR and has practised manual ventilation. We never leave an untrained worker alone with the participant.

t: We will put emergency steps in every plan that a worker can follow in seconds. They cover
x: We will put emergency steps in every plan that a worker can follow in seconds. They cover each alarm, disconnection, leak, failure, blocked airway, breathing distress and manual ventilation, and say when to call 000. The list of who to call, and when, is kept at the bedside.

t: We will keep each participant's backup equipment ready and serviced as the supplier direct
x: We will keep each participant's backup equipment ready and serviced as the supplier directs, with a power failure plan, battery run times and a move-by time. We check it every shift and test it every month. We help the participant register as a life support customer, and confirm it every 12 months. The plan covers outings.

t: We will train every worker before their first shift alone with the participant. Training c
x: We will train every worker before their first shift alone with the participant. Training covers the participant's own ventilator and plan, the NDIS Commission skills descriptor for ventilator support, and drills for incidents and emergencies. The drills include manual ventilation and power loss. A health practitioner, or a person who meets the descriptor, delivers it and signs the worker off task by task.

t: We will reassess each worker every 12 months. We also reassess before their next shift aft
x: We will reassess each worker every 12 months. We also reassess before their next shift after 3 months without supporting the participant, and after any change to the settings, the device or the clinical content of the plan. A new review date or phone number does not lapse a sign-off. A worker without a current sign-off does not work with the participant.

t: We will keep every worker within what PRO-HID-06 Decision table 3 allows. A task that need
x: We will keep every worker within what PRO-HID-06 Decision table 3 allows. A task that needs a separate sign-off is done only with it. Only the treating team or a health practitioner sets, changes or decides any clinical matter.

t: We will record only the observations the plan asks for, beside the participant's own range
x: We will record only the observations the plan asks for, beside the participant's own range. We report any reading or sign outside it to the person the plan names, straight away. We never record the oxygen the ventilator delivers as the participant's own oxygen level.

t: We will treat these as incidents under POL-INC-01 Incident Management Policy. They are a v
x: We will treat these as incidents under POL-INC-01 Incident Management Policy. They are a ventilator failure, an alarm that could not be cleared, a power loss, a disconnection with harm, a call to 000, a missed check, a mismatch and an unsigned task. We report each before the shift ends. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether an incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days.

t: We will check every participant's ventilator records for completeness every week, read a s
x: We will check every participant's ventilator records for completeness every week, read a sample every month and every record after an incident or a plan change, and act on what they show. We report the trends to the governing body every 3 months, and review this system every 12 months with participants and workers.

t: We will use standard infection precautions for every circuit, mask, humidifier and suction
x: We will use standard infection precautions for every circuit, mask, humidifier and suction task. Single-use parts are used once, parts are cleaned or changed on the dates the plan and the supplier set, and suction waste and used protective equipment are disposed of safely.

t: We will keep a training plan for each participant who uses a ventilator. It names every wo
x: We will keep a training plan for each participant who uses a ventilator. It names every worker, the training each needs, the trainer and the date it is due.

t: Ground rules
No one at [Provider name] sets or changes a value the treating team has prescribed: a mode
x: No one at [Provider name] sets or changes a value the treating team has prescribed: a mode, a setting, an alarm limit, an oxygen flow or the hours of use. A signed-off worker turns prescribed oxygen on and off at the prescribed flow, and adjusts a comfort setting, only where the sheet says so.

t: No alarm is disabled, muted or turned below the volume the plan sets. A worker pauses an a
x: No alarm is disabled, muted or turned below the volume the plan sets. A worker pauses an alarm only after the cause is fixed, only with the control the supplier's instructions give, and never leaves the participant while an alarm is paused. A participant is never left on a ventilator with the alarm silent.

t: A worker never holds a participant, and never fits a device that is not in the plan, to st
x: A worker never holds a participant, and never fits a device that is not in the plan, to stop them removing a mask or a tube. A device the treating team prescribes for a clinical purpose is used only as the plan says. The Clinical Lead and a behaviour support practitioner decide before first use whether it is a regulated restrictive practice under POL-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Policy. A hold or a device used to influence behaviour is a regulated restrictive practice and, without authorisation, a reportable incident.

t: A participant's choice to be off the ventilator, or to refuse a task, is respected. We exp
x: A participant's choice to be off the ventilator, or to refuse a task, is respected. We explain the risk, tell the treating team the same day and record it on FRM-RGT-04 Dignity of Risk Decision Record. We never force.

t: There is one plan: the treating team's. Where the participant also has a tracheostomy, POL
x: There is one plan: the treating team's. Where the participant also has a tracheostomy, POL-HID-05 Tracheostomy Management Policy and PRO-HID-04 Tracheostomy Management Procedure add rules. They do not add a second plan.

t: The equipment belongs to the participant, the treating team or the supplier. We never open
x: The equipment belongs to the participant, the treating team or the supplier. We never open or repair a ventilator or a battery, and we never lend equipment. A signed-off worker swaps external batteries, circuits, filters and humidifier chambers as the sheet and the supplier's instructions say. Only the supplier replaces a machine or an internal battery. We never use one participant's parts for another.

t: Only a signed-off worker does a ventilator task. A sign-off for one participant, one machi
x: Only a signed-off worker does a ventilator task. A sign-off for one participant, one machine or one task does not carry over to another.

t: We offer ventilator support only while ventilator management is on our certificate of regi
x: We offer ventilator support only while ventilator management is on our certificate of registration (Practice Standards Rules, section 13C).

x: Ventilator records are health information. We share them only with the participant's consent, or where the law requires or allows it. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy applies.

x: A family member who runs the participant's ventilator does so under the treating team's training. We do not direct them, and we do not ask them to do our tasks.

x: Nobody is penalised for raising a concern about ventilator safety or staffing. Reports follow POL-GOV-03 Whistleblower and Disclosure Protection Policy.

x: ventilator: a machine that moves air into and out of a person's lungs, through a mask or through a tracheostomy. It includes bilevel and CPAP machines when workers help with them. treating team: the respiratory doctor, home ventilation service or other health practitioners who prescribe the participant's ventilator and write or endorse their plan. plan: the treating team's written plan and prescription for this participant. It may sit in FRM-HID-01 Participant Health Support Plan if the team has written or endorsed it there. signed-off worker: a worker whom the trainer has signed off, task by task, for this participant and this ventilator, and whose sign-off is current. trainer: a health practitioner, or a person who meets the NDIS Commission skills descriptor for ventilator support, who trains and signs off workers. Clinical Lead: a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. alarm: a sound or message on the ventilator that tells a worker something is wrong. readiness check: the questions in Section D of FRM-HID-10. Every answer must be yes before the first shift. advance care directive: a document in which a person sets out the care they do or do not want if they cannot say so themselves. own oxygen level: how much oxygen is in the participant's blood, usually measured with a probe on the finger. It is not the oxygen the ventilator delivers. regulated restrictive practice: a restrictive practice the NDIS rules regulate, such as physical restraint or mechanical restraint. manual ventilation: moving air into the lungs by hand, with a resuscitation bag joined to the mask or the tracheostomy. move-by time: how long before a battery runs out the participant must be on other power or moved. The treating team sets it. life support customer: a customer registered with an electricity retailer and distributor because someone at the address depends on life support equipment. tracheostomy: an opening in the neck, with a tube in it, through which a person breathes. incident: has the meaning in POL-INC-01 Incident Management Policy. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives. on-call manager: the manager who takes workers' calls. In office hours this is the Service Manager. After hours it is the rostered manager. A clinical question goes to the treating team's clinical number, or to the Clinical Lead.

Ventilator Management Procedure
The result: a participant who uses a ventilator has a plan made with them and prescribed b
x: The result: a participant who uses a ventilator has a plan made with them and prescribed by their treating team. Workers are trained and signed off on their own machine. A safe response is ready for an alarm, a failure or a power cut, at any hour. This procedure gives effect to POL-HID-07 Ventilator Management Policy, C1 to C15.

t: Start this procedure: when a participant who uses a ventilator asks for our support, at st
x: Start this procedure: when a participant who uses a ventilator asks for our support, at step 1 at the start of every shift with that participant, at step 10 the moment an alarm sounds, the power fails or the participant is in trouble, at step 19 every week, every month and at each review, at step 27. Ventilator management means supporting a participant to use a machine that moves air into and out of their lungs, through a mask or through a tracheostomy. It includes the machine, its alarms and power, the mask or tube, the humidifier, oxygen if prescribed, suction and manual ventilation. It covers bilevel and CPAP machines when workers do ventilator tasks for the participant. Where the participant also has a tracheostomy, PRO-HID-04 Tracheostomy Management Procedure applies as well. There is still one plan. In this procedure, the bag means the manual ventilation (resuscitation) bag with the mask or adapter the sheet names. A business day is a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives. Who acts: The Service Manager asks the participant, gets the plan, sets the staffing rule, arranges the health review, runs the readiness check, checks every record for completeness each week and runs the monthly equipment test. In office hours the Service Manager is also the on-call manager. The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom we engage to oversee high intensity supports. They complete the ventilator sheet, make the power plan, set the training plan, read a sample of the records every month and every record after an incident or a plan change, review the monthly equipment test, and reassess workers. The treating team prescribes the settings, writes or endorses the plan and reviews the participant. We ask them. They answer to their own profession. The trainer is a health practitioner, or a person who meets the skills descriptor for ventilator support. They train workers and sign them off. The signed-off worker does every step from 10 to 26. The on-call manager takes a worker's call at any hour. In office hours this is the Service Manager; after hours it is the rostered manager. A clinical question goes to the treating team's clinical number, or to the Clinical Lead. The Quality Manager checks the system in the internal audit. In a small provider one person may hold several of these roles. A sole trader is the Service Manager and the on-call manager. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead or trainer, and cannot sign off their own competency. They engage a registered nurse or other health practitioner for both, and they need a second signed-off person before taking on the participant. Where a step says to phone the on-call manager, a sole trader phones the treating team's clinical number and writes down the time. A concern about a sole trader goes to the independent contact for concerns named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register.

t: Service Manager: Ventilator management is on our certificate of registration (Practice Sta
x: Service Manager: Ventilator management is on our certificate of registration (Practice Standards Rules, section 13C). If it is not, we do not offer this support. You know who our Clinical Lead is. You can open REG-HID-02 High Intensity Supports Register, REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register and REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register. You hold the participant's consent record (FRM-INF-01) and communication preferences (FRM-RGT-01). Signed-off worker: You are signed off for this participant, this ventilator and each task you will do. Your sign-off is in REG-HID-01. Your CPR is current. You have read the ventilator sheet, and you know where the plan, the bag, the suction and the backup are. You know the treating team's clinical numbers on the sheet and the on-call number: [on-call number]. Your phone is charged.

t: A ventilator that stops can harm a participant within minutes. Stay with them and call 000
x: A ventilator that stops can harm a participant within minutes. Stay with them and call 000. Ventilate by hand if you are signed off. Phone a manager second. Never change a prescribed setting, mode, alarm limit or oxygen flow. A wrong setting can fail to ventilate the participant or harm their lungs. Only the treating team changes them. Turn prescribed oxygen on and off, and adjust a comfort setting, only where the sheet says so. Never disable or mute an alarm, and never turn it below the volume the plan sets. Pause one only after the cause is fixed, with the supplier's control, and never leave the participant while it is paused. If you cannot hear it, you cannot answer it. An alarm that stops by itself still needs checking and writing down. Be awake and within hearing. A worker who is asleep, in another building or wearing headphones gives no protection. The staffing rule says who must be awake. A battery runs out, and a registration does not stop a power cut. Know the move-by time before you need it. Life support registration gives notice of planned outages only. A generator can kill. Its fumes are poisonous. Run it outside only. Never run it in a home, a garage or a vehicle. Oxygen feeds a fire. Keep it away from flames, heaters and smoking. Use only the flow the team prescribed. The oxygen the machine delivers is not the participant's own oxygen level. Never mix the two up. Vomit under a mask can block the airway. Take the mask off at once if the participant is sick or about to be, unless the sheet gives other steps. Never hold or restrain a participant, and never fit a device that is not in the plan, to keep a mask or tube on. It can be a regulated restrictive practice, and a reportable incident. A device the treating team prescribes is used only as the plan says, after the Clinical Lead and a behaviour support practitioner have decided what it is. Stay, reassure and phone the treating team. Never use another person's equipment, or do a task you are not signed off for. The wrong mask or the wrong setting can harm. A sign-off for one participant, one machine or one task does not carry over. Skin under a mask can break down. Look at it every time the mask is off. Tell the Clinical Lead about any sore.

Section G: the signed-off worker, when there is an outing or a power cut. Section I: the Service Manager every week and every month; the Clinical Lead every month, after any incident or plan change, and at each review. Have ready: the treating team's plan and prescription, the participant's consent record (FRM-INF-01), the supplier's instructions for the ventilator, and REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register. Rules for the record: Write in ink, or use an electronic record that locks each entry. Rule one line through a mistake, initial it and write the right entry beside it. Never erase it. Copy the plan word for word. Never fill a gap. Ask the treating team. Never change a setting. Never write a value you did not read or take. If you do not know an answer during the shift, write 'not known' and phone the on-call manager. Never guess. Every page of the record carries these lines: Blue or grey, struggling to breathe, not responding, or the ventilator cannot be made to work: call 000 now and stay with the participant. The display does not match the prescription: change nothing. Phone the treating team's clinical number on the sheet. An alarm: look at the participant first, then the circuit, then the machine. A power cut: note the time and go to backup power. Move the participant by the move-by time. An alarm you could not clear, a failure, a power cut or a call to 000: write an incident report (FRM-INC-01) before your shift ends. What happens next: the Service Manager checks every shift record for completeness each week. The Clinical Lead reads a sample every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change. The Service Manager enters the plan, consent, treating team and review dates in REG-HID-02 High Intensity Supports Register. Full pages go into the participant's file.
