t: Control
Subcutaneous injections
x: Each participant requiring subcutaneous injections receives appropriate support relevant and proportionate to their individual needs and specific subcutaneous injections and medication administered.

t: Each participant is involved in the assessment and development of the plan for their subcu
x: Each participant is involved in the assessment and development of the plan for their subcutaneous injections which includes dosage measurement and calculation. With their consent, each participant’s health status is subject to regular and timely review by an appropriately qualified health practitioner. The plan identifies how risks, incidents and emergencies will be managed, including required actions and escalation to ensure participant wellbeing.

t: There are documented written or phone orders by the health practitioner prescribing the me
x: There are documented written or phone orders by the health practitioner prescribing the medication that trained workers may administer by subcutaneous injection.

t: Appropriate policies and procedures are in place, including a training plan for workers, t
x: Appropriate policies and procedures are in place, including a training plan for workers, that relate to the support provided to participants requiring subcutaneous injections and related medication.

t: All workers have completed training, relating specifically to the participant’s injection
x: All workers have completed training, relating specifically to the participant’s injection and medication needs and high intensity support skills descriptor for subcutaneous injections, delivered by an appropriately qualified health practitioner or person that meets the high intensity support skills descriptor for subcutaneous injections. Workers must also have a basic understanding of the participant’s related health condition.

t: Subcutaneous Injections Policy
This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when a participant needs an injection
x: This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when a participant needs an injection under the skin. It is for participants, their families and advocates, our workers, and the people who check our work.

t: Every participant who needs a subcutaneous injection, in any setting: their own home, a sh
x: Every participant who needs a subcutaneous injection, in any setting: their own home, a shared home, respite, a centre or the community. Every worker, contractor, agency worker and volunteer. Only a trained worker handles injecting equipment, sets a dose or gives an injection. Every injectable medicine given by pen or pre-filled syringe, including insulin and blood thinners. A vial and syringe is covered only where the participant's plan names it. Not covered: insulin pumps and other infusions, vaccines, injections into a vein or muscle, and controlled or cytotoxic medicines. This is our choice, narrower than the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor, which contemplates pumps; a provider may widen it under a separate plan as Ground rule 7 allows. Ground rule 7 says what happens instead. This policy applies only while subcutaneous injections is set out in our certificate of registration (Practice Standards Rules, Schedule 2, clause 8(1)). If it is not, we do not take on the support and we help the participant find a provider who can. A participant who gives their own injections with no help from us keeps doing so. Commitment 2 still applies to them.

t: Commitments
We will not let a worker give or help with an injection until the participant has a curren
x: We will not let a worker give or help with an injection until the participant has a current plan from an appropriately qualified health practitioner. The plan sets the medicine and device, how each dose is measured and any dose calculation, and the sites and their rotation. It also sets the readings and limits, the action for every band of reading, storage and sharps. A plan is current until its next review date. Where the review is late, a worker injects only while the prescriber, or the health practitioner who wrote the plan, has confirmed by phone or in writing, and we have recorded, that the plan stands pending the review.

t: We will make the plan with the participant, in their usual way of communicating. We record
x: We will make the plan with the participant, in their usual way of communicating. We record what they do themselves and how they want the injection done. We start from the participant giving their own injection if they want to. We respect a refusal, and never force, trick or hide an injection.

t: We will arrange a review of the participant's health status and plan, with their consent,
x: We will arrange a review of the participant's health status and plan, with their consent, by an appropriately qualified health practitioner. We do this at least every 12 months. We ask for an earlier review within 2 business days of a trigger listed in PRO-HID-07 Decision table 5, for example a hospital stay, a severe reaction or repeated calls to the health practitioner.

t: We will make sure the plan names, for each risk, what a worker does, whom they call, how f
x: We will make sure the plan names, for each risk, what a worker does, whom they call, how fast, and when to call 000. The risks are a low or high reading, a wrong, missed or double dose, an allergic reaction, bleeding, a site reaction and a needlestick injury.

t: We will let a worker give an injection only under a current written order from the prescri
x: We will let a worker give an injection only under a current written order from the prescriber that matches the plan. If the order is unclear, out of date or does not match the plan, the worker does not give the dose and asks.

t: We will take a phone order only where the medicines law of [state or territory] allows it,
x: We will take a phone order only where the medicines law of [state or territory] allows it, and only through an order taker whom that law allows. Until the Quality Manager has recorded under Ground rule 4 the provision of that law that allows it, who may take it and the confirmation time it sets, we take no phone orders: every order comes in writing. Where phone orders are allowed, the order taker records the order, reads it back to the prescriber, and gets the prescriber's written confirmation within the time the law sets, and in any case within 24 hours. A phone order lapses if the confirmation is late. No phone order starts a medicine, changes a dose scale or a reading limit, or changes or stops insulin or a blood thinner. A phone order may hold a single dose.

t: We will limit each worker to the tasks the plan names and their sign-off lists. A trained
x: We will limit each worker to the tasks the plan names and their sign-off lists. A trained worker may give a fixed dose from a pre-filled pen or syringe. They may read a written scale, or draw up from a vial, only where the plan names that task. Only the prescriber or the plan's health practitioner decides, changes or stops a dose.

t: We will train each worker for this participant, this medicine and this device, and sign th
x: We will train each worker for this participant, this medicine and this device, and sign them off before their first unsupervised injection. A training plan names who needs which training and who delivers it. The trainer is an appropriately qualified health practitioner, or a person who meets the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor for subcutaneous injections. Each worker can explain the participant's related health condition in their own words.

t: We will assess each worker again every 12 months. A sign-off lapses after 3 months without
x: We will assess each worker again every 12 months. A sign-off lapses after 3 months without giving this participant's injection, and when the clinical content of the plan changes (a new review date or phone number does not lapse it); we assess again when it lapses, and after an error the worker's practice contributed to. A worker who is not assessed does not inject.

t: We will have a second person check independently every dose read from a scale or calculate
x: We will have a second person check independently every dose read from a scale or calculated, and every insulin or other high-risk dose where the plan says so. The plan names the second checker for each shift and how they check: in person, by phone or by video. Where no second checker can be reached, the worker phones the plan contact before the dose, follows their instruction and records it.

t: We will keep each injectable labelled for one participant and stored as its label says. We
x: We will keep each injectable labelled for one participant and stored as its label says. We will put every used needle and syringe straight into a sharps container at the point of use, and never recap. We treat a needlestick injury as an emergency: first aid, a medical review within 2 hours, and an incident report.

t: We will record every injection on the participant's medication administration record, with
x: We will record every injection on the participant's medication administration record, with the site, the reading and the units given, and every refusal. We record each reading, scale line and second check on a blood glucose monitoring record. We keep these records for 7 years (NDIS Act 2013, section 45B, from 27 August 2026: records of claims and supports are kept for 7 years).

t: We will treat every injection error, near miss, reaction and needlestick injury as an inci
x: We will treat every injection error, near miss, reaction and needlestick injury as an incident. The worker gets health advice first. We tell the prescriber or health practitioner the same day. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether the incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days. We do not punish an honest report.

t: We will check each participant's injection records every week for completeness, and the Cl
x: We will check each participant's injection records every week for completeness, and the Clinical Lead will read a sample of each participant's records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change. We audit injection practice every 6 months in the internal audit, with a desk review of the incident register and the weekly checks every 3 months. We give the governing body the trends and the improvements we recommend.

t: Ground rules
The plan holds every clinical value for the participant: each dose, scale, reading limit,
x: The plan holds every clinical value for the participant: each dose, scale, reading limit, needle length, angle, site and dose time. This policy and its procedure hold none of them. Where our document and the plan differ on a value, the plan and the current order win.

t: The plan cannot widen what a worker may do beyond PRO-HID-07 Decision table 3 and the work
x: The plan cannot widen what a worker may do beyond PRO-HID-07 Decision table 3 and the worker's sign-off. A task that is not named is not allowed.

t: For priming, air bubbles and in-use life, we follow the product information for the device
x: For priming, air bubbles and in-use life, we follow the product information for the device in the plan. We do not teach or vary it.

t: The medicines law of [state or territory] governs who may give an injection, who may take
x: The medicines law of [state or territory] governs who may give an injection, who may take a phone order, controlled medicines and storage. Where it is stricter than this policy, the law applies. When we adopt this policy the Quality Manager records what it requires, including the provision that allows a phone order, who may take one and the confirmation time it sets, or records that it allows none. They check the record every 12 months. Until that record exists, every order comes in writing.

t: An injection given mainly to influence a participant's behaviour is a chemical restraint.
x: An injection given mainly to influence a participant's behaviour is a chemical restraint. This policy authorises none. PRO-BSP-02 Regulated Restrictive Practices Procedure applies.

t: If anything is unclear, the worker does not give the dose and asks. Asking is never an err
x: If anything is unclear, the worker does not give the dose and asks. Asking is never an error.

t: Pumps, infusions, vaccines, injections into a vein or muscle, and controlled and cytotoxic
x: Pumps, infusions, vaccines, injections into a vein or muscle, and controlled and cytotoxic medicines are outside this policy. They stay with a nurse or other health practitioner. A worker takes part in a pump or an infusion only under a separate plan. The Clinical Lead and the participant's health practitioner write it, and name who does what.

t: In a small provider one person may hold several roles. The Clinical Lead is a registered n
x: In a small provider one person may hold several roles. The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom we engage to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. A sole trader never signs off their own competency and never acts as their own second checker. They use the participant's pharmacist as the chart checker. A provider with no registered nurse takes no phone orders; every order comes in writing.

t: subcutaneous injection: an injection into the fat layer just under the skin, given with a
x: subcutaneous injection: an injection into the fat layer just under the skin, given with a pen, a pre-filled syringe, or a vial and syringe. injection plan: the participant's plan for their injections, made with them and written by their health practitioner. It is held in FRM-HID-01 Participant Health Support Plan. health practitioner: a registered practitioner whose scope covers the medicine, such as a medical practitioner, a nurse practitioner or a registered nurse. For insulin it can also be a credentialled diabetes educator who is also a registered health practitioner, working with the prescriber, who sets every dose and scale. A credentialled diabetes educator who holds no registration number is recorded by their ADEA credential and the prescriber co-signs the plan. prescriber: the medical practitioner, nurse practitioner or other health practitioner who orders the medicine. written order: the prescriber's signed and dated order. A secure message, fax or email from the practice counts as written. phone order: an order the prescriber gives by phone or by word of mouth. It is recorded on FRM-HID-11 and confirmed in writing. order taker: the registered nurse, or other person the medicines law of [state or territory] allows, who takes a phone order where Ground rule 4 allows one. A worker who is not an order taker never takes an order. trained worker: a worker with a current sign-off for this participant, medicine and device in REG-HID-01. second checker: the person the plan names to check a dose independently before it is given, in person, by phone or by video. high-risk medicine: a medicine where a small mistake can cause serious harm, such as insulin or a blood thinner. The plan or the pharmacist says which of a participant's medicines are high-risk. plan contact: the person or service the plan says to phone, in hours and after hours. sharps container: a puncture-resistant container made for used needles and syringes. Clinical Lead: a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one. on-call manager: the manager rostered to take calls at any hour. In office hours this is the Service Manager; after hours it is the rostered manager. chemical restraint: the use of a medicine mainly to influence a person's behaviour. It does not include a medicine prescribed to treat a diagnosed mental disorder, a physical illness or a physical condition. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Control
Subcutaneous Injections Procedure
The result: each participant who needs an injection under the skin gets the right dose of
x: The result: each participant who needs an injection under the skin gets the right dose of the right medicine. A worker who is trained and signed off for them gives it, under a current plan and a current order. Every injection is recorded and every error is acted on. This procedure gives effect to POL-HID-08 Subcutaneous Injections Policy, C1 to C14.

t: Start this procedure when a participant needs a subcutaneous injection and wants our help
x: Start this procedure when a participant needs a subcutaneous injection and wants our help with it. Use it before the first injection, at every injection, whenever an order or the plan changes, and whenever something goes wrong. Where a Record line names a form or register that is not yet a Rise template, record the same facts in the participant's file under the same heading until it is. Where this procedure names an entry on the medication administration record (FRM-MED-01), it names the field in words; no question number of another provider's chart is used. Who acts: The Service Manager sets up the support, checks the plan and the orders, rosters workers, and checks the records every week. The participant's health practitioner writes and reviews the injection plan. The prescriber writes the orders. They may be the same person. They are usually not our workers. The Clinical Lead is a registered nurse, or another health practitioner whose scope covers the support, whom [Provider name] engages to oversee high intensity supports. They set the training plan, train and sign off workers, check the clinical items of each plan, read a monthly sample of records, give clinical advice and, when they are a registered nurse and POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 allows it, may act as order taker. Where PRO-MED-01 Management of Medication Procedure names a clinical adviser, that role is the Clinical Lead here when the adviser is a registered nurse. The order taker is the only person who takes a phone order, and only where POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 records that the medicines law of [state or territory] allows it. It is a registered nurse, or another person that law allows. The trained worker gives the injection, or helps the participant give it. A trained worker has a current sign-off for this participant, this medicine and this device in REG-HID-01 High Intensity Training and Competency Register. The second checker is the person the plan names to check a dose before it is given. The plan contact is the person or service the plan says to phone, in hours and after hours. The on-call manager takes calls at any hour. In office hours this is the Service Manager. The Quality Manager audits and reports, and, as the authorised notifier, decides whether an incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission. An injection incident is any error or near miss with an injection. It includes a wrong person, medicine, dose, device or time. It includes a missed or double dose, a dose given without the participant's agreement, a reaction, a spoiled medicine given, and any needlestick injury. In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole trader holds them all, with three limits. They never sign off their own competency. They never act as their own second checker. They never take a phone order unless they are a registered nurse and POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 allows it. A sole trader cannot be their own Clinical Lead and engages one, and asks the participant's pharmacist to be the chart checker. They name the second checker for every shift in each plan. Where a step says to phone the on-call manager, a sole trader phones the plan contact and writes down the time. A provider with no order taker, or whose Ground rule 4 record allows no phone orders, asks the prescriber to send every order in writing.

t: Trained workers: Your name is in REG-HID-01 for this participant, this medicine and this d
x: Trained workers: Your name is in REG-HID-01 for this participant, this medicine and this device, and your sign-off has not expired. You have read the participant's current plan. Its date is on the front, and its next review date has not passed. You know the plan contact's numbers, the on-call number [on-call number], and who the second checker is on your shift. You have the participant's own device and a new needle for each injection. You have a sharps container within reach, and the meter and strips if the plan needs a reading. You have the chart, clean hands and a private place the participant has agreed to. The Service Manager, before the first injection: You have the participant's agreement to the support and to health reviews (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form). You know what the medicines law of [state or territory] requires. It covers who may give an injection, who may take a phone order, controlled medicines and storage. Where that law is stricter than this procedure, follow the law. You hold the plan, and the plan holds every item below. If one is missing, send the plan back. No worker injects until it is complete. What the plan must hold: the participant's related health condition and what the medicine is for, in plain words each medicine: name, strength, device, route, times, and the date of the order that covers it how each dose is measured: the fixed dose in units, or the prescriber's written scale and how to read it a statement that no worker changes a dose, a scale or a time without a new order which tasks a worker may do: set the dose on a pen, read the written scale, draw up from a vial. Each task is named, or it is not allowed who the second checker is on each shift, and how they check: in person, by phone or by video needle length, angle, skin fold, holding time, injection sites and the order of rotation each reading the plan needs, when, the limits for low, high and call 000, and the action for every band of reading, including a reading above the target range but below the call limit. A plan with a silent band is not complete whether and when a ketone check is required, and the sick-day rules, where the practitioner sets any for each risk, the action, the contact and the time limit. The risks are a wrong dose, a missed dose, a double dose, an allergic reaction, bleeding, a site reaction and a needlestick injury how long to watch the participant after each dose storage: the fridge range, in-use life, travel, and the stock check the sharps container: who supplies it, and where it goes when full what the participant does themselves, their wishes on privacy, timing, site and communication, and what helps them feel at ease the health practitioner's name, profession and registration number, the plan date, the next review date, and the participant's consent to that review.

t: Call 000 first. Do this if the participant cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely or is fi
x: Call 000 first. Do this if the participant cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely or is fitting. Do it too for swelling of the face, lips or throat, trouble breathing, collapse or heavy bleeding. A severe allergic reaction can kill within minutes. A severe low can cause a fit or unconsciousness and needs 000 now. A dose read wrongly from a scale is a wrong dose. A wrong dose of insulin can cause a severe low that lasts for hours. Never give a dose read from a scale or calculated, or an insulin dose the plan marks for a second check, without that check. If no second checker can be reached, phone the plan contact before the dose, follow their instruction and record it. No reading, no dose, where the plan needs a reading. Insulin given without one can cause a severe low. Never give an extra or catch-up dose. A double dose of insulin or a blood thinner can cause a severe low or serious bleeding. One pen and one needle for one person. Sharing a pen, even with a new needle, can pass on a blood-borne infection. Never recap a used syringe needle. A needlestick injury can pass on infection. Step 22 says how a pen needle comes off. Heat and freezing spoil medicines. A spoiled injectable can look normal and still not work. No means no. Forcing, tricking or hiding an injection takes away the participant's right to refuse. It can also be an unauthorised restrictive practice. A phone order given to a worker is not an order. A misheard order is a wrong dose. Step 9 says what to do. A signature before the injection is a false record. It hides a missed dose from the next worker and from the prescriber.

t: Steps
Agree the support with the participant.
x: Agree the support with the participant. The Service Manager Start from the view that the participant gives their own injection if they want to. Ask what they do now, what help they want and how they like it done. Give them STA-HID-05 Subcutaneous Injections: Plain Summary, and go through it with them and a supporter they choose. Use their usual way of communicating. Ask if they agree to a health practitioner reviewing their health and plan, and to us sharing what we see with that practitioner. A guardian or other decision maker agrees only within the authority they hold. If the participant says no to either, write that down. Tell them that workers inject only under a current plan, and a plan needs its review. Offer to ask the health practitioner about other options, such as a community nurse. Never press. Ask who else should have a copy of the plan, such as family, another provider or a day service. Record their choice at FRM-INF-01. The participant has chosen the support, knows who does what, and has agreed to or declined the reviews. FRM-SUP-02; FRM-INF-01; REG-HID-02 Before the first injection support (our standard)

t: Ask the participant's health practitioner to write the injection plan with the participant
x: Ask the participant's health practitioner to write the injection plan with the participant. For insulin it can also be a credentialled diabetes educator who is also a registered health practitioner, working with the prescriber. The Clinical Lead may write the plan only if they are the appropriately qualified practitioner for this participant and medicine. Only the prescriber sets a dose or a scale. t: Check that the plan holds every item in "Before you start" and is the current plan.
x: Check that the plan holds every item in "Before you start" and is the current plan. A plan with a missing limit, contact or review date can leave a worker with nothing to follow at 2 am. The Service Manager for the administrative items, and the Clinical Lead for the clinical items Read the plan with the participant. The Service Manager checks the administrative items: the health practitioner has signed and dated it, the participant's part in it and their consent are written in it, the next review date is no more than 12 months after the plan date, and the contacts are complete. The Clinical Lead checks the clinical items: the dose and how it is measured, the needle length, angle, skin fold and holding time, the sites, the readings and limits, and that the plan states the action for every band of reading, including a reading above the target range but below the call limit. The Clinical Lead signs that check before the first dose. If an item is missing or a band is silent, send the plan back with the item named, and do not roster a worker to inject. When it is right, enter the plan date, the practitioner's name and registration number, the participant's consent and the next review date in REG-HID-02. Set a reminder 60 days before the review date. Where the plan needs a reading, attach the practitioner's own limits page as Section A of FRM-HID-12 where the plan has one; otherwise copy the limits onto Section A. Workers have a complete plan with an instruction for every band, the review date is on record and watched, and the limits are in front of the worker. REG-HID-02; FRM-HID-12 Q1 to Q11 Within 2 business days of receiving the plan, and before the first injection (our standard)

t: Put each injectable on the chart from the prescriber's written order.

The Service Manager Use PRO-MED-01 steps 2 and 3. A written order is current when the prescriber has signed and dated it, and it names the participant with two identifiers. It names the medicine, strength, dose in units or the written scale, route, frequency and what it is for. It has not passed its stop or review date. A secure message, fax or email from the practice counts as written. It must match the plan. If it does not, or anything is unclear, stop and phone the prescriber. A phone order is used only where POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4 records that the law allows it: then write FRM-HID-11 and its date as the order's source on the chart line, and mark the line "phone order, confirmation due" with the due time. PRO-MED-01 step 24 and the chart say the chart changes only from a written order, so both must be amended before the phone-order pathway is switched on. Set the chart flags: "high-risk" for insulin and any blood thinner, and "needs a route sign-off" for every injection. If the order changes the plan, ask the health practitioner to update the plan under step 2. Tell the participant what has changed. Brief each trained worker under PRO-MED-01 step 5 before the next dose. The chart, the plan and the prescriber's order all say the same thing. FRM-MED-01 (the order line: source, medicine, strength, dose, route, frequency, flags and chart checker); FRM-HID-11 Q28 to Q30 Before the first injection, and before the next dose of that medicine after any change (our standard)

t: Make the training plan for this participant.

It covers the plan's dose steps and second check, the sites and rotation, hygiene and sharps, and the readings and limits. The training follows the three headings of the NDIS Commission's skills descriptor: prepare to deliver support, implement the support plan, and review support. Name the trainer: an appropriately qualified health practitioner, or a person who meets the skills descriptor. Ask the participant if they want to show workers how they like it done. t: Train each worker on this participant, this medicine and this device.

t: Assess the worker at work, and sign them off.

t: Say you cannot take an order, and take a message.

Ask them to send it in writing, or say that our nurse will call back. Write down only the caller's name, practice and phone number. Add the time and the participant's name. Do not write down or act on any dose or medicine they say. Phone the on-call manager at once with the message. The on-call manager asks the order taker to call the prescriber back under step 10, or asks the prescriber to send the order in writing. If an order taker is on hand, pass the call to them. t: Take the phone order on FRM-HID-11.

Call the prescriber back on the practice number in the participant's file, never on a number the caller gave you. If the table says do not take it, tell the prescriber, ask for a written order, and stop. Read the whole order back, item by item, and wait for the prescriber to confirm it. If a second listener is on hand, they listen on speaker. Do not delay an urgent order to find one. Ask what to watch for, whom to phone, and how and when the written confirmation will arrive. No worker gives a dose from it. Phone the prescriber's practice and ask for the confirmation or a new written order. Ask the prescriber, the pharmacist or the Clinical Lead what to do about the next dose, and write their advice at question 27. Tell the on-call manager so the next worker knows. t: Check that you may give this injection.

Your sign-off in REG-HID-01 covers this medicine and device and has not expired. The plan's next review date has not passed, or the prescriber's confirmation that the plan stands is recorded (Decision table 4). The order on the chart matches the plan, the dose is due now and not already signed, and no phone order's confirmation is overdue. You have read the allergies and every change since your last shift. t: Confirm who the participant is.

Do this every time, even when you know them well. If you cannot be sure, do not inject. Phone the on-call manager. The injection is about to go to the right person. FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry) Before each injection (our standard)

t: Ask the participant if they want the injection now.
x: Ask the participant if they want the injection now. The trained worker Use their usual way of communicating. Say which medicine it is and what it is for. Agree a private place, and agree who does which part. Ask what helps them feel at ease. The plan lists what the participant does themselves, for example dialling the pen or choosing the site. If they say no, or show no, accept it. Do not persuade, hurry, bribe or trick. Go to the row in Decision table 4 that starts "The participant refuses". Enter the refusal code on the chart, with their reason in their own words. The participant knows what they are about to receive and has agreed, or the refusal is on record. FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry, and the refusal code and reason for a refusal) Before each injection (our standard)

t: Take the blood glucose reading, or support the participant to take it.
x: Take the blood glucose reading, or support the participant to take it. the plan says a reading is needed now, before a dose or at a set time The trained worker Let the participant take it if they want to. Wash your hands. Use the participant's own meter. Check the strips are in date and the meter shows no error. Check what the plan says about the meal. If the plan says the meal must be ready before this dose, check it. Write the reading, then compare it with the limits in Section A of FRM-HID-12 and follow Decision table 2. If the plan gives no instruction for the band the reading is in, do not decide the dose yourself: phone the plan contact before the dose, follow their instruction and record it at FRM-HID-12 Q24. If the meter shows an error, repeat once with a new strip. If there is still no reading, do not give the dose. Phone the plan contact. A used lancet goes into the sharps container. If no dose is due, stop after Decision table 2. You know the reading and what the plan says to do about it. FRM-HID-12 Q12 to Q18, and Q24 to Q27 when a call is made Before the dose, within the time the plan sets (set by the health practitioner in the plan)

t: Read the dose, in units, from the plan's written scale.
x: Read the dose, in units, from the plan's written scale. the plan says the dose comes from a written scale The trained worker whose sign-off lists reading a scale Use only the plan's current scale. Check its date matches the order. Find the line that holds the reading and read the units on that line. Write the line and the units. Never round, add, subtract, average or change the units. If the reading falls outside the scale or between two lines, or the scale is hard to read, do not guess. Phone the plan contact. If you are not signed off to read a scale, do not read it. Phone the plan contact. A fixed dose needs no calculation: the dose is the units on the chart. The dose is the number of units the prescriber's scale gives for this reading. FRM-HID-12 Q19 to Q21 Before each such dose (our standard)

t: Check the medicine and the device against the chart and the label.
x: Check the medicine and the device against the chart and the label. When the label and the chart differ, one of them is wrong. A guess can put the wrong medicine or the wrong dose into the participant. The trained worker Check the participant's name on the label, the medicine, the strength, the expiry date, and the discard date written on an opened pen. Check it looks as the product information says it should. Insulin that should be clear is clear, with no clumps, flakes or colour change. Check it was stored as the label says. If it was frozen, left in heat, or kept in a fridge outside its range, do not use it. Use only the participant's own pen or syringe. If anything does not match, stop. Phone the pharmacist and the on-call manager. The medicine in your hand is the one on the chart, in date and safe to use. FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry) Before each injection (our standard)

t: Set the dose on the device.
x: Set the dose on the device. The trained worker Wash your hands. Fit a new needle of the length the plan names. Follow the product information for the device in the plan for priming, for any air bubble and for setting the dose. Some pre-filled syringes must keep their air bubble. Decision table 6 sets what to do for each device. Set the units exactly as the chart or step 16 gives. Read the dose from the dial window or the syringe markings. Draw up from a vial only if the plan names it and your sign-off lists it. If the device sticks, leaks or will not dial, do not use it. Go to Decision table 4. The device is set to the exact dose, with a new needle. None Just before the injection (our standard)

t: Check the dose independently before it is given.
x: Check the dose independently before it is given. the dose is read from a scale or calculated, or it is insulin or another medicine the plan marks high-risk and the plan says it needs a second check The second checker The trained worker tells you the participant's name and date of birth, the medicine, the reading and the scale line if there is one. They show or read out what the device is set to. Look up the dose in the plan and the order for yourself, before you hear their number. Compare. Agree, or say what differs. If the two differ, there is no injection. Both of you read again. If you still differ, phone the plan contact. The plan names the second checker. It may be another trained worker in the room, or a registered nurse by phone or video. The participant checks their own dose only where the plan's health practitioner has written that they may. If the second checker cannot be reached, do not give the dose on your own decision: phone the plan contact before the dose, follow their instruction and record it. Go to Decision table 4. A second person has confirmed that the dose matches the plan and the order. FRM-HID-12 Q22 and Q23, or the second checker's entry on the medication administration record for another high-risk dose Before the injection (our standard)

t: Choose the site with the participant, and check the skin.
x: Choose the site with the participant, and check the skin. The trained worker Use the next site on the plan's rotation. Ask the participant if they want a different site from the list. Help them into the position the plan names, in private. Look at the skin. If it is bruised, swollen, red, hard, broken or scarred, or the site was used last time, choose another site from the list. If no site on the list is suitable, do not inject. Phone the plan contact. Clean the skin only if the plan says so. Wear gloves when you expect contact with blood or body fluid, or when the plan or our infection prevention and control plan (PLN-RSK-01 Infection Prevention and Outbreak Management Plan) says so. The injection site is the right one and the skin is fit for it. None Just before the injection (our standard)

t: Give the injection as the plan and the product information say.
x: Give the injection as the plan and the product information say. A needle that is recapped, bent or passed hand to hand can stick the person holding it. The trained worker, or the participant with your help The plan sets the needle length, angle, skin fold and holding time. Follow it. Where the plan is silent on holding time, use the product information. Tell the participant before you touch them. The participant does any part the plan lists for them. Watch the participant's face and breathing while you inject. Hold the device in place for the holding time, then take it out. Do not rub the site unless the plan says to. If the participant moves or pulls away, take the needle out safely. Never hold them down. If the needle came out early, or part of the dose may not have been given, do not repeat it. Phone the plan contact. The dose is given, or the participant has chosen to stop. None Within the time the chart allows for the dose (our standard)

t: Put the used needle or syringe into the sharps container at once.
x: Put the used needle or syringe into the sharps container at once. A used needle can injure the next person and pass on infection. Never recap a used syringe needle, and never bend or break any needle. The trained worker Keep the sharps container within reach from step 18 on, so you never carry a used needle. A used pre-filled syringe goes in whole. Take a pen needle off as the product information shows: use a safety pen needle where the plan or the pharmacist supplies one; otherwise use the outer shield only, one-handed, never the inner cap, and put the needle in the container at once. The pen stays with the participant. Never pass a used needle hand to hand. Never put a sharp in a bin, a bag or a cup. Between injections, keep the container closed, upright and out of reach of children and visitors. Close it for good at the fill line and tell the Service Manager. They replace it and arrange disposal under PRO-WST-01 Management of Waste Procedure and the sharps rules of [state or territory]. If anyone is stuck by a used needle, go now to Decision table 4. Use the row that starts "A used needle has pricked or cut anyone". No used needle or syringe is left out, and the container is safe. None Straight away, at the point of use (our standard)

t: Sign the chart with the code, the time, the reading, the units and the site.
x: Sign the chart with the code, the time, the reading, the units and the site. The trained worker Enter the code for "given" if you gave it, and the code for "self-administered with help" if the participant gave it with your help. In the notes, write the reading, the units given, the site used, and the second checker's name where one was needed. Add anything unusual. Sign only for a dose you gave or saw given. Never sign before the dose, for another worker, or from memory at the end of the shift. The chart shows what was given, where, when and by whom. FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry: date, time, code, signature and notes) Straight after the injection (our standard)

t: Watch the participant for the effects and reactions the plan lists.
x: Watch the participant for the effects and reactions the plan lists. A severe reaction or a low can start within minutes of an injection. The trained worker Stay for the time the plan sets, then keep watching for the rest of your shift. Ask how they feel and look at the site. Look for the signs of a low, a high, an allergic reaction, bleeding and a site reaction. Look for the medicine's side effects. The plan lists each one. Call 000 if the participant cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely or is fitting. Call 000 for swelling of the face or throat, trouble breathing, collapse or heavy bleeding. For anything else, follow Decision table 4 and phone the plan contact. At the end of your shift hand over to the next worker any reading outside the limits, held dose, reaction or advice you were given. If the plan is not meeting the participant's needs, or they ask for a change, tell the Service Manager the same shift. A reaction or a low is noticed at once and passed on. FRM-MED-01 (the observation note); FRM-SUP-08 The time the plan sets, then the rest of your shift (the plan; our standard)

t: Put the medicine and equipment away as the label and the plan say.
x: Put the medicine and equipment away as the label and the plan say. The trained worker Unopened pens and syringes stay in the fridge at the range on the label. A pen in use is kept as the product information says. Label it with the participant's name, the date opened and the discard date. Never freeze it. Never leave it in a vehicle or in the sun. For an outing, carry it in its case as the plan says. At the start of each shift where we hold the medicine, read the fridge thermometer. If it is outside the range, do not use the cold medicines. Phone the pharmacist and the on-call manager. Tell the Service Manager if pens, needles, strips or the sharps container will run out within 7 days. The medicine is safe for the next dose and nothing will run out unnoticed. FRM-MED-01 (the fridge temperature entry) Straight after each injection. The fridge check at the start of each shift (our standard)

t: Report the injection incident to the on-call manager and write the incident report.

Write Sections A to D of the incident report and choose "medication" as the kind of incident. Choose "other injury" for a needlestick. Report a near miss the same way. Report your own error. We do not punish an honest report. PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure then applies from step 8. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, decides whether the incident is reportable and notifies the NDIS Commission. A manager has taken charge and the incident is on record while memory is fresh. FRM-INC-01 Sections A to D; FRM-MED-01 (the administration entry notes); FRM-HID-12 Q27 Phone as soon as the participant is safe. Write the report before your shift ends (our standard). For a reportable incident the law says as soon as possible (statutory: Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules, section 19)

t: Tell the prescriber or the health practitioner about the injection incident, and ask for t
x: Tell the prescriber or the health practitioner about the injection incident, and ask for their advice. The on-call manager, or the Service Manager in office hours Phone the plan contact. Say what happened, what the participant's readings and signs were, and what was done. Ask if the plan, the order or the next doses need to change, and if the participant needs an early review under Decision table 5. Write who you told, when, and their advice. Tell the participant honestly what happened, in their usual way of communicating. Where the incident is reportable, PRO-INC-02 Reportable Incidents Notification Procedure applies. The Quality Manager, as the authorised notifier, notifies the NDIS Commission within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days. The prescriber knows, the advice is on record, and the participant has been told. FRM-INC-01 (prescriber told); REG-INC-01 (prescriber or practitioner told, date and advice) The same day (our standard). Notifying the Commission: within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days (statutory: Incident Management and Reportable Incidents Rules, sections 20 and 21)

t: Check every participant's injection records.
x: Check every participant's injection records. The Service Manager Where the Service Manager gave the injections, another manager or the Clinical Lead does this check. Read each entry since the last check in FRM-MED-01 and FRM-HID-12. Look for empty boxes and a reading outside the limits with no action. Look for a call limit reached with no call, a band the plan is silent on, and a dose read from a scale or calculated, or an insulin dose the plan marks for a second check, with no second check. Look for the same site used twice in a row against the rotation, and a phone order with no confirmation by its due time. Look for a plan or a sign-off that will expire within 60 days, a sharps container near full, and low stock. Count the calls to the plan contact. Three or more for the same reason in 7 days is a trigger in Decision table 5. Raise an incident report for any error nobody reported. Put an action that will take more than 7 days in REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register. The Clinical Lead reads a sample of each participant's records every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change, and raises any clinical concern with the plan contact. Gaps are found and fixed within a week. FRM-HID-12 Q28; REG-QMS-01 The Service Manager every 7 days. The Clinical Lead every month, and within 1 week of an incident or a plan change (our standard)

t: Ask the health practitioner to review the participant's health and plan.
x: Ask the health practitioner to review the participant's health and plan. The Service Manager Do this with the participant's consent from step 1. Ask at least 60 days before the review date in REG-HID-02. That date is never more than 12 months after the plan date. Ask within 2 business days of any trigger in Decision table 5. Send what the records show: readings outside the limits, calls, refusals, incidents and site problems. Help the participant attend. After the review, enter the date, the practitioner, the outcome and the next review date in REG-HID-02. If the plan changed, repeat steps 3 to 5 for the changed parts. Assess each worker again under step 7. No worker injects on the new plan until they are briefed. Give the new plan to the people the participant chose at step 1. If the review cannot happen before the review date, ask the practitioner for a written extension with a new date. A plan with no review and no extension is out of date. A qualified practitioner has reviewed the participant's health and plan, and the review dates are on record. REG-HID-02; FRM-HID-12 Q29 A review at least every 12 months, asked for 60 days ahead. A request within 2 business days of a trigger (our standard)

t: Audit injection practice.
x: Audit injection practice. The Quality Manager Sample participants who have injections. For each, check the plan is current and complete, and the order on the chart matches it. Check each phone order has its confirmation in time, and each worker's sign-off in REG-HID-01 is current. Check second checks are recorded, and storage and the sharps container are right, seen in person. Ask two trained workers what the participant's condition is, what a low looks like for them, and what they would do. Count injection incidents in REG-INC-01 Incident Register by type, cause, place and time of day. Report the results and trends to the governing body, with the improvements you recommend. Put each action in REG-QMS-01. Take lessons, with names removed, to team meetings. A sole trader engages the Clinical Lead to do this audit. Patterns are seen and acted on before they harm someone. REG-QMS-02 Internal Audit Schedule and Register; REG-QMS-01 Every 6 months, in the internal audit. A desk review of REG-INC-01 and the weekly checks every 3 months (our standard)

w: Phone and Verbal Medication Order Record
x: This record holds one medication order that a prescriber gives by phone or by word of mouth, for a participant who has subcutaneous injections. Only an order taker completes it, and only where POL-HID-08 Subcutaneous Injections Policy Ground rule 4 records that the medicines law of [state or territory] allows a phone order. A worker who is not an order taker never takes an order and never acts on one. PRO-HID-07 Subcutaneous Injections Procedure, step 9, says what a worker does when a prescriber calls. Who completes it, and when: Sections A to E: the order taker, during the call. Take questions 6, 10, 11, 12, 14, 21 and 22 first, while the prescriber is on the line; complete the rest from the chart straight after the call. Questions 19 and 20 are the Service Manager's. Section F: the order taker sets the due time during the call. The Service Manager completes the rest when the written confirmation arrives. Section G, and questions 19 and 20: the Service Manager, before the next dose of the medicine is due. Have ready: the participant's chart (FRM-MED-01) and plan (FRM-HID-01), the practice's phone number from the participant's file, and a pen. If a second listener is near, ask them to listen. Storage, self-management and general consent belong in the participant's medication plan (FRM-MED-02) and the participant's support plan, not here. What happens next: the Service Manager puts the order on the chart, tells the participant and briefs the trained workers. The Service Manager then checks the prescriber's written confirmation. The record is filed with the chart. Every copy of this record carries these lines: A worker who is not an order taker and is phoned an order takes a message only. The worker does not write down or act on the order. A phone order cannot start a medicine, change a dose scale or a reading limit, or change insulin or a blood thinner. PRO-HID-07 Decision table 1 lists what a phone order can and cannot do. The prescriber's written confirmation is due within the time the medicines law of [state or territory] sets, and in any case within 24 hours of the call. If it is late, the order has lapsed and no worker gives a dose from it. If you cannot read the order back to the prescriber, do not accept it. This record is used only where the Quality Manager has recorded, under POL-HID-08 Ground rule 4, the provision of the medicines law of [state or territory] that allows the order taker to take a phone order: [provision, recorded at adoption]. Where no provision is recorded, every order comes in writing.

x: This record holds each blood glucose reading for one participant. It sets each reading against the limits their health practitioner wrote in their plan, and says what was done about it. It also holds each dose worked out from a written scale, with its second check. Use one record for each participant and each plan. Start a new one when the plan changes. Who completes it, and when: Section A: the Service Manager attaches the practitioner's own limits page where the plan has one, or copies the limits from the plan once. The Clinical Lead or the health practitioner checks it, and checks that the plan gives an instruction for every band of reading, before anyone uses it. Sections B and C: the trained worker at each reading and each dose, answering only the questions the list below sets for that use. The participant may take their own reading and say the number. The worker still writes it. Section D: the trained worker, whenever a reading is outside the limits, the plan is silent for the band, a dose is held or a call is made. Section E: the Service Manager every week. The Clinical Lead reads a sample every month, and every record after an incident or a plan change. Have ready: the plan (FRM-HID-01), the order on the chart (FRM-MED-01), and the participant's own meter and strips. Have the written scale too if the plan uses one. Never copy a scale onto this record. Read it from the plan. What happens next: the Service Manager reads this record every week and checks the pattern. A page is filed in the participant's file when it is full. When, and which questions to complete: A routine reading inside the target range with no dose due: questions 12 to 18. A reading before an insulin or other high-risk dose: questions 12 to 18, then 22 and 23 where the plan requires a second check. A dose read from a scale: questions 12 to 23. A reading below the low limit, at or above the call limit or in a band the plan is silent on, a held dose, or any call: also questions 24 to 27. Questions 1 to 11 are completed once per page. Every page of this record shows the practitioner who set the limits, the limits themselves, and who to call (Section A). It also carries these lines: Cannot be woken, cannot swallow safely, fitting, trouble breathing or swelling of the face or throat: call 000 now. No reading, no dose, where the plan needs a reading. A reading below the low limit, or at or above the call limit: stop and follow the plan. If the plan gives no instruction for the band you are in, phone the plan contact before the dose. Never guess a dose and never change one.

t: practitioner: in this policy, an NDIS behaviour support practitioner who works for us. The
w: Behaviour Support in the NDIS Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: practitioner: in this policy, an NDIS behaviour support practitioner who works for us. The Commissioner considers the person suitable to do behaviour support assessments, including functional behavioural assessments. The Commissioner also considers them suitable to develop plans that may contain restrictive practices (the Rules, section 5). suitability outcome: the Commission's written decision on a person's application to be a practitioner. It says suitable, not suitable or unable to decide. It shows the date, the pathway used (self-assessment or new entry-level) and any conditions. It shows no capability level. For a new entry-level practitioner the Commission writes separately to say it will reconsider the outcome after 12 months. capability level: the level a practitioner self-assesses against the Positive Behaviour Support Capability Framework, endorsed in writing by their clinical supervisor. The four levels are core, proficient, advanced and specialist. The Commission does not issue or endorse levels, so the level is never read from the suitability outcome. clinical supervisor: a practitioner, inside or outside [Provider name], who is at proficient level or above on their own endorsed self-assessment and trained in clinical supervision, and who provides clinical supervision. Clinical Lead: the most senior clinical supervisor, who owns clinical practice at [Provider name] (POL-SBS-03 defines the role). In a sole practitioner provider, the external clinical supervisor. clinical supervision: planned supervision of a practitioner's own work by a more experienced practitioner. It looks at their assessments, plans and decisions. It is not line management. work practice: each kind of work a practitioner does for us. It covers assessments, interim and comprehensive plans, reviews, consultation, authorisation and lodgement steps, and the handover and coaching of the people who carry out plans. caseload: every participant a practitioner has open work for. regulated restrictive practice: one of the five practices the Rules cover (section 6). Seclusion is sole confinement where the person cannot leave, such as a locked room. Chemical restraint is medicine given mainly to change behaviour. Mechanical restraint is a device that stops or limits movement, such as a strap or bed rails used for behaviour. Physical restraint is force used to stop or limit movement. Environmental restraint limits free access to parts of the person's environment, such as a locked cupboard or fridge. functional behavioural assessment: the process of working out the purpose behind a person's behaviour. interim behaviour support plan: the first plan, written for a participant with an immediate need. comprehensive behaviour support plan: the full plan that follows a behaviour support assessment, including a functional behavioural assessment. implementing provider: a provider that carries out a participant's behaviour support plan. start-up session: the first clinical supervision session, held before the practitioner is given any participant. suitable list: the list in REG-HRM-02 of practitioners released to be given participants. It shows their outcome date, pathway, endorsed capability level, conditions and any reconsideration letter date. new entry-level pathway: the Commission's suitability pathway for a person with less than 6 months of behaviour support experience or a limited portfolio of evidence. The Commission reconsiders the outcome after 12 months, by letter. The practitioner keeps working during the reconsideration unless the Commission tells them otherwise. file number: the number we give a participant's record. Supervision records use it in place of a name. participant: in this policy, any person with disability we provide supports or services to. the Commission: the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission. The Commissioner is its head. independent contact for concerns: in a provider with one owner, the outside person who receives concerns about the owner. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.
