The external Clinical Supervisor, engaged in writing and named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register, does step 27 and also step 28, the Service Manager's check on the practitioner's own work. PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) and POL-SBS-07 use this clock for an interim plan and set no other handover time. In this procedure: The Restrictive Practices Rules means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. w: Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure
x: A plan that contains a restrictive practice has not made the practice authorised. Authorisation comes from the state or territory. If you tell a provider that a practice is authorised and it is not, a worker may use it without authority. The participant may be harmed, and the use is a reportable incident. Do not use this template, an old copy or memory for a state or territory rule. The rules change and differ in each place. Take the rule from our dated state or territory note. A wrong rule leads to a wrong use. Telling is not understanding. A person who nods may not have understood. A worker who misunderstands a strategy can use it wrongly and harm the participant. Attendance is not competence. A worker who signed the sheet may still be unable to carry out the plan. Their provider trains and observes them against the plan and confirms it to you in writing. You observe a sample, and every worker who will apply a physical restraint protocol. Tell the provider in writing what an untrained worker may and may not do. An untrained worker does not apply a physical restraint technique or an as-needed practice, and calls the provider's on-call manager instead. Removing a continuous restraint because a worker is untrained can itself cause the harm the plan prevents. Share only what the participant agreed to. Sharing the plan without consent breaches privacy. It can put the participant at risk if a family member is the concern. Teach a physical technique only if you are qualified to teach it. Write the note's last-checked date and the outcome. If anything is unclear, ask the authorising body, and tell no one the practice is authorised until you can confirm it. The practitioner The participant already holds the plan. Now explain its reasons. Use the supports in FRM-RGT-01. Offer a trusted supporter, a break or two shorter sessions. Say what the behaviour tells us the participant needs, what the plan aims for and why each strategy is there. Ask what the participant thinks and write their words. If a person decides for the participant by law, explain to that person too. If the participant does not seem to follow, try another way and record what you tried. The participant has heard the reasons for their plan and has had a say. FRM-SBS-04 Q8, Q9 and Q11 Within the handover clock (our standard)

Ask the provider to keep the card where its workers see it at the start of a shift. t: Explain to each provider how each practice is authorised and the conditions on its use.

t: Agree with the implementation contact who holds each reporting duty.
w: Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure
x: Agree with the implementation contact who holds each reporting duty. The practitioner Give the contact the reporting summary and go through it duty by duty. If you gave a written notice under PRO-SBS-02 step 27, start from it and add anything missing. Duty 1: report each use of a regulated restrictive practice to the NDIS Commissioner every month. Use the Commissioner's approved form (Restrictive Practices Rules s 14(1)(a) and (2)). While a short term approval from the state or territory is in force, report every 2 weeks instead (s 14(1)(b)). The Commission expects the monthly report within 5 business days after the end of the month, and expects the provider to activate the lodged plan and lodge evidence of authorisation in the NDIS Commission Portal (Commission guidance, not the Rules). Duty 2: keep a written record of each use for 7 years (s 15). Duty 3: lodge evidence of authorisation with the Commissioner as soon as reasonably practicable after a use (s 9(2)(b)). Duty 4: tell us when circumstances change, so we can review the plan (s 10(2)(b)), and tell us of any emergency or unauthorised use within 1 business day (our standard). Duty 5: if a practice is used and no plan covers it, take all reasonable steps to have an interim plan within 1 month. Take the same steps for a comprehensive plan within 6 months (s 11 to s 13). Duty 6: report a use that is not authorised, or not in line with the plan, as a reportable incident. The time runs from when the provider becomes aware. Notify the Commissioner within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days (Incident Rules s 16, s 20 and s 21; Commission guidance on harm). Advise the 24 hour route for any injury or medical check, and whenever in doubt. If the plan has no restrictive practice, say that it allows none and that any use must be reported. If the provider is not registered, say that these duties bind registered providers. Tell it that the law of the state or territory and the NDIS Code of Conduct still apply to it. If the plan contains a regulated restrictive practice and the provider is not registered for supports that involve one (the Registration Rules s 7(2)), tell the Clinical Supervisor the same business day and start the concern route in PRO-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure (Decision table 3). t: Use this form to record what we explained, taught and agreed with the people who carry out
w: Behaviour Support Plan Handover and Training Record
x: Use this form to record what we explained, taught and agreed with the people who carry out a participant's behaviour support plan. It is the proof that we handed the plan over, trained people in it and kept supporting them. The behaviour support practitioner who holds the plan completes it. Open one running record for each implementing provider for each version of the plan, and one for the support network. Add a dated entry for each contact. A contact is any meeting, session, visit or call listed at question 2, and questions 2 and 3 are answered for each entry. Questions 1 and 4 are answered once per record. Answer Sections A, B and I every time. Answer the other sections when the contact covered them. The heading of each section says when. If you do not know an answer, write "Not known" and the date you will find out. Never leave it blank. When | Complete these questions Handover (the first contact with a provider or the support network): questions 1 to 13; 14 to 17 where the plan has a regulated restrictive practice; 18, 19 and 29 to 32. Training, coaching or mentoring: questions 1 to 6, 20 to 25 and 29 to 32. Catch-up for a new or absent worker: questions 1 to 6, 13, 23, 25 and 29 to 32. Restrictive practice training oversight: questions 1 to 4 and 26 to 32. Check-in or advice on a barrier: questions 1 to 4 and 29 to 32. Briefing on a changed plan: questions 1 to 4, 11 to 13, 17 where the authorisation changed, and 29 to 32. For a version that changes only the version number and the review date: questions 1 to 4, 13 and 31. Have these ready: the plan, with its number, version and the date it was given out, from REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register the participant's consent record, FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form the participant's communication preferences, FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form the instructions and guidance you wrote for the plan for a plan with a regulated restrictive practice, our note for each state or territory of use (kept in REG-QMS-03 Compliance Obligations Register) for the same plan, the participant's authorisation outcome from REG-SBS-01 the authorisation summary and the reporting summary. These six answers decide what you do next. Do that step before you close the record. A provider at question 10 that has not accepted its part: use the first item under "If it goes wrong" in PRO-SBS-03. A practice at question 17 that is not approved: use Decision table 1 in PRO-SBS-03. "Needs coaching" at question 23: go to PRO-SBS-03 step 15. "Needs changes" or "Not acceptable" at question 27: go to PRO-SBS-03 step 19. Any barrier at question 29: give it an action, an owner and a due date at question 30 (PRO-SBS-03 step 22). Any choice at question 32 other than "nothing further": go to PRO-SBS-03 step 24. What happens next: you sign the record and file it within 2 business days of the contact. The Service Manager then copies the answers named in the question protocol to REG-SBS-01 within 2 business days. PRO-SBS-03 Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure sets each step. When systems are down, use a paper copy. Enter it within 2 business days after the system is back.

t: behaviour support plan: a written plan that sets out how we will support a participant's b
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Policy
x: behaviour support plan: a written plan that sets out how we will support a participant's behaviour, build their skills and improve their quality of life. It is either interim or comprehensive. interim plan: a plan written quickly for an immediate need, while the full assessment is done. PRO-SBS-06 sets its own clocks. comprehensive plan: the full plan, written after a behaviour support assessment that includes a functional behaviour assessment. regulated restrictive practice: one of five practices the Rules name. Seclusion is being shut in a room or space. Chemical restraint is a medicine given to manage behaviour. Mechanical restraint is a device, such as straps or bed rails, used to stop movement. Physical restraint is holding a person still. Environmental restraint stops free access, for example a locked cupboard or gate. A medicine a doctor prescribes to treat a diagnosed condition, or to allow treatment to happen, is not chemical restraint. A device used for treatment, and a reflexive hand that guides a person away from harm, are not restraint either (the Rules, section 6). Practitioner: an NDIS behaviour support practitioner. This is a person the Commissioner considers suitable to carry out behaviour support assessments and write behaviour support plans (the Rules, section 5). A contractor who meets this test is a Practitioner. Clinical Supervisor: the person who supervises a Practitioner's work and checks each review. In a provider with one Practitioner, this is someone outside [Provider name]. Clinical Lead: the senior Practitioner who owns clinical practice at [Provider name]. Quality Manager: the person who decides whether to notify the Commissioner of a concern or a reportable incident, and sends the notice. In a sole practitioner business, the Practitioner, who makes that decision with the Clinical Supervisor. implementing provider: a provider whose workers carry out the plan and may use a regulated restrictive practice. monitoring check: a look at how the plan is working, using the participant's views and the data. It cannot change the plan. review: a full test of the plan by a Practitioner. It can change the plan. scheduled review: the review due at least every 12 months. early review: a review started sooner because something changed. review date: the day the Practitioner signs the review decision. in-force date: the day the Practitioner finalises and signs a version of the plan. person who decides for the participant: a guardian, a parent of a child, or another person with legal authority to decide for them. They take part. They never replace the participant. support network: the family, carers, guardian, advocate and friends the participant agrees to include. data: the records an implementing provider keeps about behaviour, skills and any use of a restrictive practice, as the plan sets. concern: a situation where an implementing provider cannot be engaged effectively, or is not carrying out the plan. Commissioner: the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commissioner. The Commission is the body the Commissioner leads. lodge: give a plan to the Commissioner in the form and way the Commissioner requires. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Start when a plan is due a check or a review. Start also when a trigger in Decision table 2 arrives, or when you see a concern about an implementing provider. This procedure is for a specialist behaviour support provider. An implementing provider uses PRO-BSP-07 Behaviour Support Plan Review Procedure for its own part. An interim plan is checked here every month. PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) sets its other clocks. PRO-BSP-03 Functional Behaviour Assessments and Behaviour Support Plans Procedure writes each new version of a plan. This procedure hands over to it at step 20. Who acts: The Practitioner reviews the plan and decides the changes. Only a Practitioner the Commissioner considers suitable may do this (the Rules, sections 5, 17 and 22). The Clinical Supervisor checks each review before it is final. The Clinical Supervisor also gives a written view on any notice to the Commissioner. The Clinical Lead owns this procedure. The Clinical Lead and the Chief Executive are told the same day of any date at risk. The Service Manager keeps REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register and opens the monthly records. The Service Manager gives each plan a Practitioner and cover, lodges reviewed plans, and closes concerns. The Quality Manager checks the register and the records every month, decides whether to notify the Commissioner of a concern, and sends the notice. In a sole practitioner business, the Practitioner holds the Service Manager, Clinical Lead, Quality Manager and Chief Executive roles and does what those roles do, with two exceptions. The external Clinical Supervisor, named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register, does the Service Manager's checks on the Practitioner's own work, and makes the decision at step 24 with the Practitioner. The Practitioner sends the notice at step 25. Where a step says to tell another role, the Practitioner writes it on the plan row and tells the Clinical Supervisor.

x: You hold the role named at the step. You have the current plan, the last record and the participant's communication preferences (FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form). You have the participant's consent record (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form). You can open REG-SBS-01 and FRM-SBS-05 Behaviour Support Plan Review Record. You have read the Commission's current guidance on lodging a plan, and the Commissioner's current approved form. You have a contact, and that contact's manager, for each implementing provider. For step 22, you have a login to the NDIS Commission Portal, or the route the Commission has told you to use. For step 25, you have the Commission's contact centre email address and phone number (1800 035 544), and the contact for the behaviour support team of the participant's state or territory.

t: A late review leaves the plan out of date. For a plan with a regulated restrictive practic
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: A late review leaves the plan out of date. For a plan with a regulated restrictive practice, a review after the due date breaches a condition of our registration (the Rules, section 22(b); the Act, section 73J). It does not void the plan. The plan remains the plan in force and must still be followed until the new version is finalised. Tell each implementing provider so, in writing. A check cannot change a plan. If a check shows the plan must change, start a review. A change made at a check has no clinical check and does not reset the review date. Missing data is not "no behaviour". Reading a gap as a quiet month hides harm and makes a reduction look safe when it is not. Only a prescriber changes a medicine. You may propose a reduction of a chemical restraint. You never change a dose. A practice with no authority is an unauthorised use. If an authorisation ends or is refused, the provider must stop using the practice. Continued use is a reportable incident (the Act, section 73Z(4)(f)). Information goes only to people the participant agreed to. Sending a plan to someone who has no consent is a privacy breach. Telling the provider is not telling the Commissioner. A call to the provider's manager does not meet the duty at step 25. Safety comes before paperwork. If anything you see suggests harm, abuse or neglect, stop. Follow PRO-SGD-01 Violence, Abuse, Neglect, Exploitation and Discrimination Procedure and PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure first.

t: Check whether workers are applying the plan as written.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Check whether workers are applying the plan as written. The Practitioner Use fidelity data, what you have seen, what workers and the participant told you, and incident reports. Where the data cannot answer, ask to watch the plan being applied, with the participant's consent. Answer Yes, Partly, No or Cannot tell. If the answer is Partly or No, use Decision table 3 and go to step 23 when it says so. You know whether the plan is carried out, or where it is not. FRM-SBS-05 Q15 With step 9 (our standard)

t: Start the incident review under PRO-SBS-05.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Start the incident review under PRO-SBS-05. The provider that used the practice may have to report it to the Commission. A late call from us can delay that report. a regulated restrictive practice was used in an emergency, without authorisation or outside the plan The Practitioner Pass the notice as PRO-SBS-05 step 1 sets: tell the Service Manager and the Quality Manager what you found, who told you and when. The Quality Manager opens an FRM-SBS-06 record under PRO-SBS-05 Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) and names you as lead, unless your own plan is in question. Tell the provider's manager that the use may be a reportable incident, if the provider has not already treated it as one. Do not wait for step 9. The use is in an incident review, and the provider knows its duty to report. FRM-SBS-05 Q16 The same business day you find out (our standard)

t: Decide, for each practice, whether it can be reduced or ended.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Decide, for each practice, whether it can be reduced or ended. the plan contains a regulated restrictive practice The Practitioner Look at the use this period, counting each as-needed (PRN) administration given for behaviour as a use, the positive change recorded, and what the participant and others said. Choose one: remove it, reduce how often, reduce how long, trial without it, or no change. A decision of no change needs a reason. It also needs a date to look again, no later than the next check. For a chemical restraint, only the prescriber changes the medicine, so send your proposal to the prescriber with the participant's consent. A reduction or an end to a practice starts a review. Do this together with the progress check in PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support), and make one entry in each record. Every practice has a recorded reduction decision, with reasons. FRM-SBS-05 Q22, Q24, Q25, Q26, Q27 At every check and every review (our standard)

t: Decide whether this check, or a request, needs an early review.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Decide whether this check, or a request, needs an early review. The Practitioner Use Decision table 2. A request from the participant, or from the person who decides for them, always starts a review. If a trigger applies, open an early review record, or change Q3 to Early review, and answer Section A. Then go to step 14. If none applies, set the date of the next check, no later than Decision table 1 allows, and list the follow-up actions. Every trigger is answered and the next date is set. FRM-SBS-05 Q1 to Q6, Q46, Q47 Answer a provider's request within 1 business day. Decide within 2 business days of the trigger (our standard). The law says a review follows a change as soon as practicable (statutory: the Rules, section 22(a))

t: Test the plan against the review questions.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Test the plan against the review questions. The Practitioner Answer Q19 to Q21 and Q23. If the functional behaviour assessment no longer explains the behaviour, start a new or updated assessment under PRO-BSP-03 and carry on with what you know. If the plan no longer fits at all, start a new plan under PRO-BSP-03. Check that each regulated restrictive practice still meets the conditions in the Rules (section 21(3)). You know what in the plan no longer fits. FRM-SBS-05 Q19, Q20, Q21, Q23 A scheduled review: start 3 months before the due date. An early review: start within 5 business days of the trigger, or the same business day where someone is at risk (our standard)

t: Decide the changes to the strategies, each tied to evidence.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Decide the changes to the strategies, each tied to evidence. The Practitioner Name the data or the participant's words behind each change. Change the environment before you add a restriction. If you change nothing, write why the plan still fits. A list of proposed changes, or a recorded decision that the plan still fits. FRM-SBS-05 Q28 A scheduled review: within 10 business days of step 14. An early review: within 5 business days of step 14, or 2 where someone is at risk (our standard)

t: Talk the proposed changes through with the participant first.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Talk the proposed changes through with the participant first. The Practitioner Show the participant the proposed changes in a form they understand and ask what they think. Then ask the people they agreed to, and each implementing provider that will apply the changes. Change the proposal where their views show a problem, and say what you changed. Keep minutes on the participant's file, and invite only people the participant agreed to. The people affected had a say before the new version is written. FRM-SBS-05 Q31 A scheduled review: within 10 business days of step 15. An early review: within 4 business days of step 15, or 1 where someone is at risk (our standard)

t: Start the consultation and authorisation steps in PRO-SBS-02.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Start the consultation and authorisation steps in PRO-SBS-02. A practice added without authorisation is an unauthorised use from its first day. a change adds, alters, extends or ends a regulated restrictive practice, or an authorisation ends before the next review The Practitioner Before the new version is final, give the participant and their family or guardian the details of the intention. Use an accessible format (the Rules, section 20(4)). Consult the provider that will use the practice. Follow the authorisation process where the participant lives. Record each authorisation and its end date. For an added, altered or extended practice, the new version is not final until PRO-SBS-02 Restrictive Practices Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) is done. Where only an end date is near, finalise the new version and run the renewal alongside. Every changed practice has consultation and authorisation behind it. FRM-SBS-05 Q29, Q30, Q32 Start within 2 business days of step 15 (our standard). Authorisation takes the time the state or territory process sets

t: Decide how soon the next review should be.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Decide how soon the next review should be. The Practitioner Ask whether the participant's needs, situation or progress call for a review sooner than 12 months. Think about changing behaviour and a new implementing provider. Give your reason either way. The next review is never more than 12 months after this one. The next review date is set, with a reason. FRM-SBS-05 Q33 Before the record goes to the Clinical Supervisor (our standard)

t: Check the record.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Check the record. The Clinical Supervisor For a review, read this record and the proposed changes before the review decision is signed. Check each change has evidence, the participant was heard, and each restrictive practice has consultation and authority. Accept it or return it with the changes needed. For a monitoring check, read the record at the next supervision session. Read every record for a plan with a regulated restrictive practice, and at least 1 in 5 of the rest. A second qualified person has tested the Practitioner's judgement. FRM-SBS-05 Q34 A scheduled review: within 5 business days of receiving the record. An interim plan: within 2 business days. An early review where someone is at risk: within the at-risk times in Decision table 2. A monitoring check: at supervision, within 3 months (our standard)

t: Sign the review decision, and start the new version of the plan.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Sign the review decision, and start the new version of the plan. The Practitioner Sign and date the decision. The date is the review date. Every review ends with a new version of the plan, even when nothing changes. Start it under PRO-BSP-03. That procedure sets how the new version is drafted, shared for acceptance, authorised, checked, finalised and given out. Where a change needs authorisation, record "pending authorisation" on the plan row (REG-SBS-01, authorisation) and in the draft's restrictive practice schedule, and do not finalise or lodge the new version until authorisation is granted. The current plan stays in force until the new version is finalised. A fix to spelling or layout is not a review. Record it as an addendum and leave the dates as they are. The review is done, and the new version is under way. FRM-SBS-05 Q35 Within 2 business days of the Clinical Supervisor accepting the record, or the same day where someone is at risk (our standard). An early review: within 20 business days of the trigger, or 5 where someone is at risk (our standard). A scheduled review: on or before the due date (statutory for a plan with a regulated restrictive practice: the Rules, section 22(b))

t: Start the change briefing and any training for the new version under PRO-SBS-03.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Start the change briefing and any training for the new version under PRO-SBS-03. The Practitioner Check each person's consent first. A person with no consent gets nothing. The participant is briefed first, in their way, then the support network they agreed to, then each implementing provider. Say what changed and why. Use STA-BSP-01 Behaviour Support and Restrictive Practices: Plain Summary to explain their rights. If the participant says no to a provider that must apply a changed strategy, do not send it. Tell the Clinical Supervisor the same day, and talk with the participant about what a "no" means for their supports. Decide which changed strategies need training. A changed strategy starts only after the people who apply it are trained, and a regulated restrictive practice only after it is authorised. Write the in-force date at Q35, the briefing records at Q36 and the training decision at Q37. Everyone who holds the plan has been told what changed, participant first, and anyone who needs training has a date. FRM-SBS-05 Q35, Q36, Q37; FRM-SBS-04 Each holder receives the new version within 1 business day of it being finalised. The briefing and any training are complete within the handover clock in PRO-SBS-03: 5 business days, or 2 for an interim plan (our standard)

t: Lodge the reviewed plan with the Commissioner when Decision table 4 says so.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Lodge the reviewed plan with the Commissioner when Decision table 4 says so. The Service Manager Use the lodging step in PRO-BSP-03, and lodge once. Use the form the Commissioner has approved and the route the Commission requires (the Rules, section 23(1) and section 24(3)). Lodge it whether or not state or territory authorisation has been given (section 24(2)). Write the reference at Q38. If Decision table 4 says lodging is not required, write "Not required" and the reason. Tell the Practitioner the date it was lodged. The Commission holds the current plan, or the record says why it does not. FRM-SBS-05 Q38 Within 5 business days of the new version coming into force (our standard). The law says as soon as practicable (statutory: the Rules, section 24(1))

t: Raise the concern, and ask the provider's manager in writing to put it right.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Raise the concern, and ask the provider's manager in writing to put it right. The Practitioner Use Decision table 3. Write what you saw, with dates. Ask the manager to reply within 5 business days and to fix it within 10. A written request sent at step 6 counts. If the participant is at risk, phone the manager the same day, then write, and ask for a reply within 1 business day. Tell the Service Manager the same day. Add Section H to the record that is open, or open a new record with Q3 set to Concern only and answer Section A. The provider has had a clear, written chance to put it right. FRM-SBS-05 Q1 to Q6, Q39, Q40 Within 1 business day of the concern arising. The same business day where the participant is at risk (our standard)

t: Decide whether to notify the Commissioner.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Decide whether to notify the Commissioner. The Quality Manager Read Q39 and Q40. Ask the Clinical Supervisor for a written view first. The Clinical Supervisor gives it within 2 business days. If it has not come by then, decide without it and say so. Use Decision table 3. If the Quality Manager is involved in the concern, the Chief Executive decides. A "do not notify yet" needs a written reason and a date to look again. A decision, with a reason and its author, is on record. FRM-SBS-05 Q41 Within 2 business days of the Clinical Supervisor's view. At once where the participant is at risk (our standard)

t: Notify the Commissioner in writing.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Notify the Commissioner in writing. The Quality Manager Say who we are and who the participant is. Name the plan and its version, and the implementing provider. Say which concern it is, what we saw with dates, and what we did to put it right. Say if anyone is at risk. Send it in writing by email to the Commission's contact centre, or to the behaviour support team for the participant's state or territory. Where the participant is at risk, phone the Commission (1800 035 544) first, then write. There is no portal function for this notice. No rule sets a form or a time for it, so the time here is our standard. Keep a copy and the Commission's acknowledgement. Write the reference at Q42. If no acknowledgement arrives within 5 business days, phone the Commission and write a file note. The Commissioner knows. FRM-SBS-05 Q42 Within 1 business day of the decision (our standard)

t: Tell the participant and the implementing provider about the notice.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Tell the participant and the implementing provider about the notice. The Practitioner Tell the participant first, in their way: what we told the Commission, why, and that their supports go on. With their consent, tell their support network. Tell the provider's manager in writing, unless the Commission or a risk to someone says not to. Nobody learns of the notice by surprise. FRM-SBS-05 Q43 Within 2 business days of the notice (our standard)

t: Answer each request from the Commissioner and carry out each agreed action.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Answer each request from the Commissioner and carry out each agreed action. The Practitioner Log each request with its due date, and tell the Service Manager the day it arrives. The Act gives at least 14 days to provide information the Commission asks for. It allows a shorter time only where there is a risk of serious harm (section 73F(2)(i) and (3)). If you cannot meet a date, ask the Commission in writing for more time before it passes. Keep supporting the provider to put the problem right. Every request is answered on time, and the work agreed with the Commission is done. FRM-SBS-05 Q44 By the date the Commission sets (statutory: the Act, section 73F(2)(i)). Where it sets none, within 5 business days (our standard)

t: Close the concern.
w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: Close the concern. The Service Manager Close it when two things are true. The Commission has told us it needs nothing more from us. The next check shows the plan is carried out, or engagement works, or the participant no longer uses that provider. Write what ended it. Enter any lasting improvement in REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register. Until then, read the concern each month. The concern has an outcome and a date. FRM-SBS-05 Q45 Within 2 business days of the closing conditions being met. Read it each month while it is open (our standard)

For a comprehensive plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice this is statutory (the Rules, section 22(b)). For every other plan it is our standard, from the Quality Indicators Guidelines, section 42 (5). Count 12 months from the review date, which is the day the Practitioner signed the last review decision, or from the new version's in-force date, whichever is earlier (our standard; the Commission counts from the plan start date). If there has been no review, count from the in-force date. An interim plan's review date is the comprehensive plan's due date, never 12 months. A scheduled review starts 3 months before the due date, so that the new version is also in force by then (our standard). Decision table 2: Does a trigger need an early review? If this happens Then Time The participant, or the person who decides for them, asks for a review Start a review. We never refuse Standard times Anyone may be at risk of harm now Phone the provider the same day. Agree interim safety measures. Start the review At-risk times The behaviour changes: a new behaviour, or a clear rise or fall in how often, how intense or how long over two data periods Start a review Standard times The participant's health, home, housemates or workers change, or a new provider will carry out the plan Start a review Standard times The participant moves to another state or territory Start a review. Authorisation rules differ in each state and territory Before the move where we know of it. Otherwise standard times An implementing provider tells us of a change in circumstances (the Rules, section 10(2)(b)) Answer, then decide using the other rows Answer within 1 business day A regulated restrictive practice was used in an emergency, without authorisation or outside the plan Follow PRO-SBS-05 first. Review the plan when the incident review is done Start within 5 business days of the incident review An authorisation ends, is refused or changes its conditions Tell the provider the same day it cannot use the practice without authority. Start a review Call the same business day. Then at-risk times A regulated restrictive practice is reduced or ended Start a review, so the plan matches what now happens Start within 5 business days A significant incident involving the participant's behaviour, such as an injury, a hospital visit or police Start a review. Use the incident record as data Standard times Two checks in a row show no progress, or things getting worse Start a review Standard times The participant is progressing faster than the plan expected Start a review to look at reducing the plan or ending it Standard times We take over the participant from another specialist provider Confirm the plan is current, has been lodged and shows each practice correctly. The review due date carries over. Start a review at once if it falls within 3 months Within 5 business days of taking over None of these No early review. Set the next check date Not applicable All the times in this table are our standard. The law says a review follows a change as soon as practicable (the Rules, section 22(a)). Standard times: decide within 2 business days of the trigger. Start within 5 business days. Sign the review decision at step 20 within 20 business days of the trigger. At-risk times: start the same business day. Sign the review decision at step 20 within 5 business days of the trigger. Where step 17 applies, the new version waits for the state or territory authorisation process. Agree interim safety measures with the provider for that time. Decision table 3: Does the Commissioner need to be told? If Then We contacted the provider on three different days over at least 10 business days, with one written request to its manager, and got no data or reply Cannot engage effectively. Go to step 23. The written request at step 6 counts, so step 24 follows at once The provider refuses to send data, to talk with us or to take part in a review Cannot engage effectively. Go to step 23, then step 24 at once We cannot find anyone at the provider to talk to Cannot engage effectively. Go to step 23, then step 24 at once Data is missing for two checks in a row, whatever the reason given Cannot engage effectively. Go to step 23. Step 24 follows when the provider has had 10 business days after our written request Workers do not apply the strategies as written Plan not carried out. Go to step 23. Step 24 follows if the provider has not put it right by the date in our written request A regulated restrictive practice is used outside the plan or without authorisation Plan not carried out. PRO-SBS-05 also applies. Go to step 23. Step 24 follows at once if the provider refuses to act, or if it happens again after our advice The provider says it will not apply a strategy Plan not carried out. Go to step 23, then step 24 at once The provider is not registered for supports that involve a regulated restrictive practice (the Registration Rules, section 7(2)) Plan not carried out lawfully. Go to step 23, then step 24 the same day The participant is at risk of harm because the plan is not carried out Notify now. Go to steps 23 and 24 the same day. Do not wait for any date in this table None of these No concern. Keep working with the provider, and look again at the next check Decision table 4: Does the reviewed plan go to the Commissioner? After the review Then The plan contains a regulated restrictive practice, with or without changes Lodge it. The Rules name a reviewed plan (section 24(1)). Where nothing changed, lodge the current plan with the review date (our standard) The review removed the last regulated restrictive practice Lodge the revised plan, so the Commission's record shows the practice has ended (our standard) The plan has no regulated restrictive practice and never had one Lodging is not required, because the Rules apply to a plan that contains one (section 24(1)). Write "Not required" at Q38

w: Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure
x: If Then A review will be late, or is late Tell the Service Manager the same day. The Service Manager tells the Clinical Lead and the Chief Executive the same day. Add a row to REG-QMS-01 Continuous Improvement Register. Tell the participant. Tell each implementing provider in writing that the plan remains in force and the review is under way. Sign the review decision within 10 business days, using the data you hold, and lodge as normal. The Chief Executive decides whether to self-report the breach to the Commission. Never change the due date in the register to hide it. The law lets nobody extend a limit it sets The Practitioner is away, leaves, has a conflict with the participant, or is no longer a person the Commissioner considers suitable The Service Manager names another Practitioner within 2 business days. The Service Manager hands over every open record. Tell the participant who it is. A sole Practitioner arranges another suitable Practitioner in writing before any planned absence that covers a due date, and tells the Clinical Supervisor The participant will not take part, or cannot Follow step 7. A "no" is respected and recorded. Check the plan on the data and the views of others, and offer a second way at the next check An implementing provider will not send data or help Follow steps 6 and 23. Do not stop checking the plan The Clinical Supervisor returns the same review twice, or you disagree Ask for a second clinical opinion from outside within 5 business days. The due date does not move. If it is within 5 business days, sign the version the Clinical Supervisor accepts and tell the Clinical Lead The Clinical Supervisor cannot check the record within the time in step 19 A second NDIS behaviour support practitioner named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register checks it within the same time. Ask the Clinical Supervisor to read the proposal before you decide The authorising body refuses or delays authorisation for a changed practice Tell the Clinical Supervisor. POL-GOV-03 Whistleblower and Disclosure Protection Policy protects you You are worried about a colleague or a manager, for example a delayed review, a delayed notice, or pressure to change a finding Tell the Clinical Supervisor. POL-GOV-03 Whistleblower and Disclosure Protection Policy protects you You see signs of harm, abuse or neglect Stop. Follow PRO-SGD-01 and PRO-INC-01. Come back to this procedure when the participant is safe The participant moves to another provider Follow PRO-SUP-04 Transitions to or from a Provider Procedure. Give the new Practitioner the plan, the last records and the review due date. The due date carries over The portal is down, or lodging fails Phone the Commission on 1800 035 544 and write a file note. Try again each business day. Write the delay and its reason at Q38. Do not let the 5 business days pass without a note The participant or their family complains about the plan or a check Follow PRO-FBK-01 Feedback and Complaints Management Procedure. The complaint does not pause a review The Commission asks for something we cannot give in time Tell the Service Manager. Ask the Commission in writing for more time before the date passes (step 27) Systems are down Use paper copies of FRM-SBS-05. Enter them within 2 business days after systems are back

t: Use this record each time we check or review a participant's behaviour support plan, or ra
x: Use this record each time we check or review a participant's behaviour support plan, or raise a concern about an implementing provider. It shows what the participant told us, what the data showed, what we changed and who we told. The Practitioner who holds the plan completes it. Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses it. A provider that only implements plans uses FRM-BSP-06 Behaviour Support Plan Implementation Review Record. Open one record for each of these: a monitoring check, due at least every 1, 3 or 6 months under Decision table 1 in PRO-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Monitoring and Review Procedure a scheduled review, due at least every 12 months an early review, when something changes for the participant a concern only, when an implementing provider cannot be engaged or is not carrying out the plan. When | Complete these questions (the minimum set for each use): A monitoring check: questions 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 14, 15, 16, 46 and 47. Add question 9 only when the participant could not be engaged, and question 13 only when data is missing, late or unreliable. When the plan contains a regulated restrictive practice, add questions 22, 24 and 25, and question 26 for a "no change" decision. A scheduled review or an early review: every question in Sections A to G and I. Add Section H where a concern is found. A concern only: Sections A, H and I. A concern found during a check or review: add Section H to that record. Write "Not applicable" in the first question of a section you skip. "The Rules" here means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. Four answers send you to a step in PRO-SBS-04. A "Yes" at Q16 goes to step 11. A "Partly" or "No" at Q15 goes to Decision table 3. A "Yes" at Q29 goes to step 17. Any concern at Q39 goes to steps 23 to 28. Keep the record open until that step is done. Have ready: the current plan and the last record the data from each implementing provider the participant's communication preferences (FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form) the participant's consent record (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form). What happens next: the Service Manager updates REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register and closes the record. PRO-SBS-04 sets each step. When systems are down, use a paper copy and enter it within 2 business days after they are back.

t: We collect this information to check that the participant's plan is working and to change
x: We collect this information to check that the participant's plan is working and to change it when it is not. It includes health and behaviour information, which is sensitive. The Practitioner, the Clinical Supervisor, the Service Manager and the Quality Manager read this record. We tell the participant what we found. We share changes with implementing providers and the support network only with consent, or where the law requires it. The law requires us to lodge a reviewed plan with the Commissioner when it contains a regulated restrictive practice. We may also give the Commissioner facts about a concern under Section H. The participant can ask to see this record and ask us to correct it. We keep it for at least 7 years from the review date, and longer where the participant is a child or a state or territory law requires it. We give the Commissioner the facts about a concern under Section H when we notify it, and the reviewed plan when the law requires lodgement. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store it.

t: The Practitioner files the record on the participant's file and gives it to the Service Ma
x: The Practitioner files the record on the participant's file and gives it to the Service Manager within 1 business day of completing it (our standard). For a monitoring check, the Clinical Supervisor reads the record at the next supervision session, and within 3 months at the latest (our standard). For a scheduled review or an early review, the Practitioner sends this record and the proposed changes to the Clinical Supervisor. The Clinical Supervisor decides within the time in step 19 of PRO-SBS-04. For a concern, the Practitioner tells the Service Manager and the Quality Manager the same day. The Quality Manager follows steps 24 and 25 of PRO-SBS-04, and the Service Manager follows step 28. The Service Manager checks that every question that applies is answered. Then the Service Manager updates REG-SBS-01 and closes the record, within 2 business days of receiving it (our standard). A record for a review stays open until the new version is in force. The Quality Manager checks the records and the register every month. The Service Manager sends anything overdue to the Clinical Lead and the Chief Executive the same day. The Service Manager reads every open concern each month. A sole Practitioner files the record and updates REG-SBS-01 themselves. Their outside Clinical Supervisor does the check, and makes each decision on a concern with them. Keep each record for at least 7 years from the review date (our standard). A longer time applies for a child, or where state or territory law sets one.

w: Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: This policy sets out what [Provider name] does when a provider uses a regulated restrictive practice in an emergency, or without authorisation. It covers a participant whose behaviour support plan we write or review, or are engaged to write. We support the provider that used the practice, and we include the participant in the review of what happened. It is for participants, their families and advocates, the providers that implement our plans, our practitioners and the people who check our work.

t: Every practitioner, Clinical Supervisor, manager and contractor who works for [Provider na
w: Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: Every practitioner, Clinical Supervisor, manager and contractor who works for [Provider name] under our registration for specialist behaviour support. Every participant we hold a plan for, or are engaged to write one for. For any other participant, we give the caller the safety and reporting advice in PRO-SBS-05 steps 4 and 9 without recording identifying details, and we offer the referral route in PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support). We open no review for a participant we are not engaged for. Every implementing provider: a registered provider, an unregistered provider, or a person who supports the participant day to day. It does not set the duties of the provider that used the practice. That provider makes the incident report, the notification to the NDIS Commission and the record of the use. A provider that also implements plans follows POL-BSP-07 Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Policy (Implementing Behaviour Support Plans) for its own uses. "The Incident Rules" in this policy means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018. "The Restrictive Practices Rules" means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018.

x: We will advise the implementing provider on what follows a use. The advice covers the participant's safety and medical check, and working with emergency and health services. It covers notifying the NDIS Commission in the time the Incident Rules set: within 24 hours of becoming aware where the incident involves the death, serious injury, abuse or neglect, unlawful sexual or physical contact or sexual misconduct of a participant, or an unauthorised restrictive practice that resulted in harm; otherwise within 5 business days. t: regulated restrictive practice: one of five practices the Restrictive Practices Rules, sec
w: Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: regulated restrictive practice: one of five practices the Restrictive Practices Rules, section 6, name. They are seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint and environmental restraint. A locked cupboard, a medicine given mainly to change behaviour and a bed rail used to stop someone getting up are everyday examples. emergency use: a use of a regulated restrictive practice in an unplanned emergency, to stop serious harm, when no plan and no authorisation covered it. The Restrictive Practices Rules say "single emergency use" in section 9(2)(a) and do not define it. unauthorised use: a use that the authorisation of a state or territory did not cover, or that went outside the participant's behaviour support plan. implementing provider: the provider, or the person, who supports the participant day to day and uses, or may use, a practice under the plan. practitioner: an NDIS behaviour support practitioner, a person the Commissioner considers suitable to assess and to write plans (the Restrictive Practices Rules, section 5). Clinical Lead: the senior Practitioner who owns clinical practice at [Provider name]. In a sole practitioner business, the Practitioner. Clinical Supervisor: the experienced Practitioner who supervises a Practitioner's work and signs off each review. In a sole practitioner business, always someone outside [Provider name], engaged in writing. Quality Manager: the person who decides whether to tell the NDIS Commission about a provider or a reportable incident, and sends the notice. In a sole practitioner business, the Practitioner, who makes that decision with the Clinical Supervisor. interim plan past its end date: an interim plan whose end date has passed without a comprehensive plan or a new version replacing it. A comprehensive plan does not lapse: a late review is a breach of our registration conditions, not a lapse, and the plan stays in force until the new version is finalised. reportable incident: one of six types the NDIS Act 2013, section 73Z(4), names. One type is the use of a restrictive practice other than in accordance with an authorisation of a state or territory. authorisation: the approval that the law of a state or territory requires before a practice may be used. It is not our advice and it is not a plan. review: our check of one emergency or unauthorised use. It is not a plan review. plan review: the formal review of a plan by a practitioner. PRO-SBS-04 sets it. concern route: the steps in PRO-SBS-04 that ask a provider in writing to put a problem right, and decide whether to tell the Commissioner. support network: the family, friends, carers, advocates and others the participant chooses. person with legal authority: a guardian, a nominee or another person the law allows to decide for the participant. independent advocate: a person outside [Provider name] who speaks up for the participant's wishes and rights. debrief: the meeting where the implementing provider's workers and managers work out what to learn and change. The provider writes down what came out of it. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives. When we advise a provider on a time limit in the Incident Rules, we tell it to count every weekday, so the notice is never late.

For any other participant, give the caller the safety and reporting advice in steps 4 and 9 without recording identifying details, offer the referral route in PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support), and open no review record. An implementing provider must tell a specialist provider when a change in circumstances means the plan needs review (the Restrictive Practices Rules, section 10(2)(b)). We may also hear from the participant, a family member, an advocate, another provider, the NDIS Commission, or the data in a plan review. Who acts: Any worker who is told passes the notice on (step 1). The Service Manager receives the notice, names the lead practitioner and the cover, and keeps the incident review entry in REG-SBS-01. The practitioner supports the provider, includes the participant and leads the review. This is the NDIS behaviour support practitioner who holds the participant's plan. The Clinical Supervisor reads the findings and signs them off. The Quality Manager opens the review record, watches the time limits, decides whether to tell the NDIS Commission about a provider under PRO-SBS-04, and closes the record. The Chief Executive decides a concern when the Quality Manager is involved in it. In a sole practitioner business, the practitioner holds the Service Manager, Quality Manager and Chief Executive roles and does what those roles do, with two exceptions. The external Clinical Supervisor named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register does the Service Manager's checks on the practitioner's own work, signs off every review, and makes any reportable-incident decision, and any decision to tell the NDIS Commission about a provider, with the practitioner. The cover practitioner named there takes notices when the practitioner is away. The independent contact for concerns hears any concern about the practitioner. If our own worker used the practice, we are the provider that used it. Start with PRO-INC-01 Incident Management Procedure, FRM-INC-01 Incident Report Form and PRO-INC-02 Reportable Incidents Notification Procedure. A provider registered for plan implementation also follows PRO-BSP-08 Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Procedure (Implementing Behaviour Support Plans). t: Our advice is not an authorisation. Only the process of [state or territory] authorises a
w: Reportable Incidents Involving the Use of a Restrictive Practice Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: Our advice is not an authorisation. Only the process of [state or territory] authorises a practice. A provider that hears "carry on" from us may keep using a practice that nobody has authorised. The provider's clock started before ours. The provider's time to notify runs from when it became aware (the Incident Rules, sections 20(1)(a) and 21(1)(a)). We may hear on day 3 or on day 6. Check the date and advise at once. A participant who is hurt needs help first. Do not wait for facts, forms or a manager. Waiting can make an injury worse. A review can hurt the participant a second time. Asking someone to go over a restraint before they are ready causes distress and loses their trust. The participant chooses the time and the way. What the participant says belongs to them. Sharing it with the provider, family or others without consent breaks their trust and can break privacy law. A single emergency use can still mean the plan must change. Do not close a review because the use looks like a one-off. We are not the participant's treating health practitioners. Never say that no medical check is needed. Never advise on a medicine dose. Do not coach a physical hold over the phone: physical techniques are taught only by a qualified trainer under PRO-SBS-03 Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure.

t: Service Manager: copy each answer marked for REG-SBS-01 to the incident review entry withi
x: Service Manager: copy each answer marked for REG-SBS-01 to the incident review entry within 2 business days of receiving it (our standard). Practitioner: complete Sections C and D within 12 business days of the notice (our standard). Practitioner: complete Q30 and Q31 within 15 business days of the notice (our standard). Clinical Supervisor: sign the findings and the outcome within 2 business days of Q31 (our standard). Quality Manager: complete Q36 within 5 business days of the follow-up check, and close the record within 2 business days after that (our standard). File the record on the participant's behaviour support file. Keep it for 7 years from the day it is closed (our standard). That period matches the 7 years from the day a record is made in the Incident Rules, section 12(4), and the Restrictive Practices Rules, section 15(3). Other law can require longer, for example for a record about a child. Check the law of [state or territory] before any record is destroyed.

t: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when a participant needs behaviour su
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: This policy sets out what [Provider name] commits to when a participant needs behaviour support urgently, before a full assessment is possible. It is for participants, their families and advocates, the providers who support them, our Practitioners and the people who check our work.

t: Every participant we are asked to help, or find, who has an immediate need for behaviour s
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: Every participant we are asked to help, or find, who has an immediate need for behaviour support. This includes a participant whose providers are using, or are likely to use, a regulated restrictive practice that no behaviour support plan covers. Every Practitioner, Clinical Supervisor, manager and worker of [Provider name], contractors included, who takes part in an interim plan. Every setting: the participant's own home, a shared home, a day service, a school, a hospital or the community. Specialist behaviour support only. A provider that only implements plans uses POL-BSP-08 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Implementing Behaviour Support Plans).

t: Commitments
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)

t: We will decide the urgency of every referral within 1 business day, using the bands in PRO
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will decide the urgency of every referral within 1 business day, using the bands in PRO-SBS-06. A referral that is not an immediate need goes to the right pathway the same day, and we tell the referrer why.

t: We will answer in writing every referral that needs an interim plan. For danger now we ans
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will answer in writing every referral that needs an interim plan. For danger now we answer the same business day, and for urgent within 2 business days. If we cannot take it, we say so in that time and help the referrer find another specialist behaviour support provider.

t: We will put safety first. Where anyone is in danger now, we tell the referrer to call 000
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will put safety first. Where anyone is in danger now, we tell the referrer to call 000 before we ask anything else. We check what keeps people safe until the plan is issued. We do this on the day we accept for danger now, and within 1 business day for urgent.

t: We will use only a Practitioner, an NDIS behaviour support practitioner whom the Commissio
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will use only a Practitioner, an NDIS behaviour support practitioner whom the Commissioner considers suitable, to evaluate the risk and write the plan. That includes any contractor we engage. A Clinical Supervisor checks every interim plan before it is issued.

t: We will record an engagement date on the day we accept a referral. We will issue the inter
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will record an engagement date on the day we accept a referral. We will issue the interim plan within 5 business days of it for danger now, and within 10 for urgent. Where a regulated restrictive practice is involved, we will never issue it later than 1 month after the engagement date. We will issue the comprehensive plan within 6 months of it; 84 days is our target. An interim plan's review date is the comprehensive plan's due date, never 12 months. The Service Manager checks every open plan against these dates at least every week.

t: We will involve the participant in evaluating the risk, in the way they choose. We show th
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will involve the participant in evaluating the risk, in the way they choose. We show them the draft plan before it is final. We give them their copy in a form they can use, and we explain it. We do this within 1 business day of issuing the plan, and before we tell anyone else.

t: We will involve every provider that carries out the participant's supports in evaluating t
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will involve every provider that carries out the participant's supports in evaluating the risk and in considering the draft plan. We also take account of earlier assessments, and of what family, carers and other services tell us, with the participant's consent.

t: We will evaluate the risk the behaviour poses to the participant and to others, and what m
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will evaluate the risk the behaviour poses to the participant and to others, and what may be driving it, before we write any strategy. We rate each risk and record it.

t: We will write each interim plan on the Commissioner's approved form, or on another form th
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will write each interim plan on the Commissioner's approved form, or on another form that section 23(1) of the Rules allows and that holds every required item. Its content follows the Commission's Interim Behaviour Support Plan Checklist (October 2025): it is brief and usable; it evaluates the risk of harm; it does not include a functional behaviour assessment; it sets out changes within the environment; for any restrictive practice it says what is used, when, why, how and by whom; and it says how advice, guidance and support will be given. Its strategies are evidence-based, person-centred and proactive. They address the participant's needs and the likely reason for the behaviour, and give the participant chances to build skills and join in community life.

t: We will include a regulated restrictive practice in an interim plan only if it is authoris
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will include a regulated restrictive practice in an interim plan only if it is authorised, or is on the state or territory's interim or short term authorisation pathway, and the plan identifies it clearly and states its authorisation status. Where authorisation is not yet in place, the plan says the practice must not be used, and says what happens until authorisation is granted. The plan also says how the practice will be reduced and ended. It must also meet every test in the Rules: last resort, least restrictive, in proportion to the risk and for the shortest time. We never include a practice that the state or territory prohibits.

t: We will give the participant, and their family, carers, guardian or other relevant person,
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will give the participant, and their family, carers, guardian or other relevant person, the details of any intention to include a restrictive practice. We do this in a format they can use, before the plan is final.

t: We will lodge every interim plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice with the C
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will lodge every interim plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice with the Commissioner within 5 business days of finalising it. We lodge it whether or not authorisation is in place.

t: We will give each implementing provider the issued plan and its point-of-care card, and br
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will give each implementing provider the issued plan and its point-of-care card, and brief its manager, within 1 business day of issuing the plan. We complete the handover, training and guidance within the interim handover clock in PRO-SBS-03 Supporting the Implementation of the Behaviour Support Plan Procedure: 2 business days from issue. We check that they can follow it. Only with the participant's consent, we give the same guidance to their support network in the same time.

t: We will check how the plan is working within 7 days of issuing it. After that we check it
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: We will check how the plan is working within 7 days of issuing it. After that we check it at least every 1 month, as PRO-SBS-04 sets. We review the plan early when it is not working. When the need is over, we replace the plan with a comprehensive plan or close it, and record why.

x: An interim plan never waits for the full assessment. The functional behaviour assessment belongs to the comprehensive plan, under PRO-BSP-03 Functional Behaviour Assessments and Behaviour Support Plans Procedure.

t: The engagement date is the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a reg
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: The engagement date is the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a regulated restrictive practice was first used and led to the referral, whichever is earlier (our standard). The Commission treats a provider as engaged from the service agreement date, or a later start date the agreement names, so our date is never later than the Commission's. Our written acceptance states that it is the start date for developing the plan for the purposes of the Rules, section 19, and the service agreement (AGR-SUP-01 Service Agreement Template) records the same date. We do not wait for a signed service agreement. PRO-BSP-03 sets the general rule.

t: Where a regulated restrictive practice is in use or likely, we apply the 1 month and 6 mon
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: Where a regulated restrictive practice is in use or likely, we apply the 1 month and 6 month limits in section 19 of the Rules. The Rules set them where a practice has been used and we are engaged as a result. We apply them to a likely practice too. This is our standard.

t: the Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour S
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Policy (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: the Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018. the Incident Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018. interim behaviour support plan: a plan written quickly to manage the risk of a participant's behaviour until a comprehensive plan replaces it. immediate need: the participant's behaviour puts them or others at risk of harm now or soon, and no plan manages it. It also covers a regulated restrictive practice in use, or likely to be used, that no plan covers. urgency band: the group a referral is placed in: danger now, urgent, not immediate, or covered by a current plan. PRO-SBS-06 sets them. comprehensive behaviour support plan: the full plan that follows a behaviour support assessment and a functional behaviour assessment. Practitioner: an NDIS behaviour support practitioner. The Commissioner considers this person suitable to do behaviour support assessments and write plans that may include restrictive practices. Clinical Supervisor: an experienced Practitioner who checks the Practitioner's work and supports their practice. Clinical Lead: the senior Practitioner who owns clinical practice at [Provider name]. implementing provider: a provider whose workers carry out the participant's supports and will carry out the plan. support network: the family, carers, friends, advocates and others the participant chooses. regulated restrictive practice: seclusion, chemical restraint, mechanical restraint, physical restraint or environmental restraint, as the Rules define them (the Rules, section 6). A locked cupboard is environmental. A bed rail used to stop movement is mechanical. A medicine given mainly to change behaviour is chemical. authorisation: the permission a state or territory gives, through its own process, for a regulated restrictive practice. Some states and territories have no such process. interim pathway: a state or territory's short term or interim authorisation route for a practice that must be used before full authorisation can be decided, where the state or territory has one. engagement date: the date we agree in writing to develop the plan, or the date a regulated restrictive practice was first used and led to the referral, whichever is earlier. The clocks in the Rules, section 19, run from it. lodge: send to the Commissioner, in the form and the way the Commissioner requires. issued: finalised and in force, on the date the Practitioner signs the plan. Issued, finalised and in force mean the same date in this policy and in PRO-SBS-06. guidance: teaching and coaching on how to carry out the plan, with a check that it was understood. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Call 000 first. If anyone is in danger now, the referrer calls 000 before anything else. O
w: Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support)
x: Call 000 first. If anyone is in danger now, the referrer calls 000 before anything else. Our phone line cannot keep a person safe, and every question asked first costs time. Do not advise a restrictive practice by phone. Advice to use one, with no plan and no authorisation, can make the provider's use unauthorised. The provider may then have to report it as a reportable incident. The clock starts at engagement, not at the plan. The 1 month limit runs from the engagement date. Missing it breaches a condition of our registration (Rules, s 19(2)(a)). That can lead to a civil penalty (NDIS Act 2013, s 73J). The other provider's clock may end sooner. Its 1 month limit runs from the first use of the practice. Step 8 tells it the date. The law is in the Rules, s 11(2), s 12(2) and s 13(2). An interim plan does not wait for the full assessment. The functional behaviour assessment belongs to the comprehensive plan (Rules, s 20(5)). Holding the interim plan back for it leaves the risk unmanaged. Never write an unauthorised practice as allowed. A worker who reads "allowed" will use it. The provider then uses a practice with no authority. Sharing without consent breaches privacy. It can also put the participant at risk, for example if a family member is part of the concern.

t: Describe the behaviour and what is happening around it.

FRM-SBS-07 Q14 and Q15 Within 2 business days of the engagement date for danger now, and within 4 for urgent (our standard)

t: Rate the risk to the participant and the risk to others.

x: Rate the risk to the participant and the risk to others. Practitioner Write one line for each person or group who could be harmed. FRM-SBS-07 Q16 and Q17; REG-SBS-01 (risk of harm) Within 2 business days of the engagement date for danger now, and within 4 for urgent (our standard)

t: Ask the participant's treating practitioner to check for a health cause.

A health cause is looked for alongside the plan, and the evaluation has a finish date. t: Interim Behaviour Support Risk Evaluation
Use this record for every interim behaviour support plan. It shows how we decided the plan
x: Use this record for every interim behaviour support plan. It shows how we decided the plan. It records the urgency, who we talked to, the risks, what we agreed and what we did to put the plan to work. The plan itself is written on the Commissioner's approved form (FRM-BSP-02 Behaviour Support Plan Cover Sheet and Lodgement Record). This record does not replace it. This record authorises no restrictive practice. Only the authorisation process of the state or territory can do that. Only a specialist behaviour support provider uses this record. A provider that only implements plans uses FRM-BSP-08 Interim Behaviour Support Engagement Record. This record holds only what is new in an interim plan. The referral, the engagement date, the Practitioner and the consent are on FRM-SBS-03 Functional Behaviour Assessment Report Template. The cover sheet FRM-BSP-02 holds the plan's checks, acceptance and lodgement. FRM-SBS-04 Behaviour Support Plan Handover and Training Record holds the handover. FRM-SBS-05 Behaviour Support Plan Review Record holds the monthly checks. Do not write the same answer twice. Who completes it: Section A: whoever takes the referral starts it. The Clinical Lead and the Service Manager finish it. Sections B to G: the Practitioner, as each step of PRO-SBS-06 Interim Behaviour Support Plans Procedure (Specialist Behaviour Support) is done. Q30: the Practitioner records it, and the Service Manager closes the record. Answer the questions in section D only when the answer to Q4 shows a practice. Each question in section D is answered once for each practice. Have ready: the referral and any earlier plans. Have the participant's communication preferences (FRM-RGT-01 Communication, Advocacy and Support Preferences Form). Have their consent record (FRM-INF-01 Consent to Collect, Use and Share Information Form). Have the authorisation schedule in REG-QMS-03 Compliance Obligations Register. Three answers open the next step. A band of "Not immediate" or "Covered by a current plan" at Q2 sends the referral to another pathway. A practice at Q4 opens section D and the lodgement duty. A band of "Danger now" opens the 000 call at Q3. What happens next: the Service Manager copies the answers marked for REG-SBS-01 Behaviour Support Plan Register to the plan row. This is within 2 business days of the stage, as the register's entry rules set. PRO-SBS-06 sets every step. When systems are down, use the paper copy. Enter it in the system within 2 business days of the system coming back (our standard).

t: We collect this information to work out how to keep a participant and other people safe. W
x: We collect this information to work out how to keep a participant and other people safe. We use it to write an interim plan and to help those who carry it out. Some of it is health information, which is sensitive. The Practitioner, the Clinical Supervisor and the Service Manager read this record. We give the providers who carry out the plan the parts they need. We share with a participant's support network only what the participant agreed to. We lodge a plan that contains a regulated restrictive practice with the NDIS Commissioner, because the law requires it. If you are the participant, you can ask to see this record and ask us to correct it. You can have an advocate with you. You can tell us you disagree, and we will write it down in your words. To complain, use POL-FBK-01 Feedback and Complaints Management Policy. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets how we store this record and how long we keep it.

Where the family chooses a key worker, that person is the plan lead. practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners. continuity arrangement: what the family agreed will happen when a session or practitioner has to change. interruption: any change or break in a child's supports, planned or unplanned. interim safety action: a step taken straight away to keep a child safe while a concern is looked into. reportable incident: one of the six types named in the NDIS Act 2013, which we must notify to the NDIS Commission. PRO-INC-02 lists them. Incident Rules: the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018. independent contact for concerns: in a sole trader's business, a person outside the business who receives a concern about the sole trader. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.
