t: The Child Procedure (Early Childhood Supports)
The result: each child's rights are explained and used every day. Each type of setting has
x: The result: each child's rights are explained and used every day. Each type of setting has a safety assessment, and each child has agreed controls, before a practitioner sees the child. A worry about a child's safety is reported on the day. When a session or practitioner changes, the child's supports carry on the way the family agreed. This procedure gives effect to POL-ECS-02 The Child Policy (Early Childhood Supports). Steps 1 and 2 give effect to C2, C4, C5 and C6. Steps 3 and 4 give effect to C1 and C3. Step 5 gives effect to C12. Step 6 gives effect to C13. Steps 7 to 9 give effect to C2 and C6. Steps 10 to 25 give effect to C7 to C11. Steps 26 to 30 give effect to C14. "The Incident Rules" means the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Incident Management and Reportable Incidents) Rules 2018. Every concern about a child has a record in FRM-ECS-01. A concern is also an incident only where the harm is connected with the provision of our supports or with one of our workers (the Incident Rules, sections 9, 15(2) and 20(1)); it then also has one incident report (FRM-INC-01) and one row in REG-INC-01 Incident Register. A concern about harm at home or elsewhere that is not connected with our supports is a child protection report, not an NDIS incident: FRM-ECS-01 Section A holds the practitioner's account and no NDIS Commission notice is made. Decision table 2 makes the split.

When a session or practitioner has to change: steps 26 to 30. Who acts: The practitioner at the session, for every session and every concern. The plan lead, for the first session, plan reviews and changes. The Service Manager, for checks, observation, the setting-type safety assessments and unplanned changes. The child safety lead, for every concern after the worker's call. The deputy acts when the lead is away or is the subject. The Quality Manager, as authorised notifier for the NDIS Commission. The Chief Executive, when a concern is about one of our workers, managers or owners. A sole trader is the plan lead, the child safety lead and the worker. They name a deputy and an independent contact for concerns in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register. The independent contact receives any concern about the sole trader. t: A duty to report can be yours alone. The law of [state or territory] can make you personal
x: A duty to report can be yours alone. The law of [state or territory] can make you personally responsible. Waiting for a manager can leave a child at risk and put you in breach of the law. Questions can weaken a child's account. A leading question can damage what the child later tells police or child protection. A promise of secrecy cannot be kept. You will have to tell someone to keep the child safe. The child then loses trust in you. Telling the wrong person can put the child at risk. Telling the person a concern is about can lead to more harm. It can also lose evidence. The NDIS Commission notice and the child protection report are two separate duties. One does not replace the other. The Commission's 24 hour clock runs from the first time any manager knows, day or night (our standard; the Rules say from when the provider becomes aware). A photograph of a child's body can add to their distress and harm the case. Keep evidence as it is, unless police or child protection direct otherwise.

x: Check that each worker named for the child is cleared, has signed the code of conduct and is trained. For this child, read the assessment for each setting type the child will be seen in, then agree a short controls line with the family (FRM-CHS-02 Part B, two or three lines): one to one support, personal care, transport, online contact, photographs and who else will be there. t: The plan lead opens the row within 2 business days of the family accepting our offer (our
x: The plan lead opens the row within 2 business days of the family accepting our offer (our standard). The Service Manager names the plan lead that day. Use one row for each child. Brothers and sisters each get their own row, linked in column AF. Fill columns A to G and I before the first session. Column J stays blank until a record exists. The first session does not go ahead while column I is empty for the type of setting it is in. Fill columns H and Y by the end of the first session. Fill every other column within 2 business days of the form or meeting that produces it (our standard). Write "not yet asked" with a date when a required answer is not known. Ask at the next contact with the family. Never overwrite or delete an entry. A correction is a new version of the row, with the date, your name and the reason. Columns H, N, R, X, Z, AH, AI, AJ and AK hold dated entries. Add each new entry underneath the last one. Column AL holds one date, replaced at each check. The family's own words stay in the forms (FRM-ECS-02, FRM-ECS-03, FRM-ECS-05). This register holds dates, names, counts, record numbers and one-line pointers. Where a short phrase of the family's is entered, such as "none wanted" in column N, it is entered as it was said, signed or shown. Nobody tidies it. Column J takes record numbers only. Never write what was seen, said or suspected in this register. When the plan lead is away for more than 5 business days, the Service Manager names another worker to keep the row. When the system is down, complete the paper forms. Enter the row within 1 business day of the system coming back. A sole trader is the plan lead and keeps every row. A row is closed only when all of these are true: column AD is filled and column AC says "exited" the family has their final progress report and their copy of the last plan column AA shows the handover was given, or the family's decision that none was wanted every consent line in column Q has a withdrawn date or an end date nothing in column AE, AI, AJ, AK or AL is still due.

t: The plan lead and the key worker can see the rows of the children they work with. The Serv
x: The plan lead and the key worker can see the rows of the children they work with. The Service Manager, the Quality Manager and the Chief Executive can see every row. A worker can see columns B, E, G, M, P, S, U and Y for the children they see. They cannot browse the register. Column J shows record numbers only. Only the child safety lead, the deputy and the Chief Executive can open the forms behind those numbers. A person with parental responsibility can ask to see their child's row and ask us to correct it. We answer within 10 business days (our standard). Before a row is released, the child safety lead checks columns E and J. Nothing is released that an order forbids or that could put the child at risk. Another provider in the team receives only what column Q allows. An auditor or the NDIS Commission sees rows only as the law allows or requires. Rows hold sensitive personal and health information about children. Keep the register in [system name], with a login for each person and a log of changes. Lock away any paper form. POL-INF-01 Information Management Policy sets the wider privacy rules.

This policy sets how [Provider name] works with the family of each child who receives earl
x: This policy sets how [Provider name] works with the family of each child who receives early childhood supports from us. The family's knowledge, strengths, culture and choices lead every plan. It is for families, our workers and the people who check our work.

t: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. The family is
x: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. The family is the parents, carers and other people who raise the child, as the family describes itself. x: We will ask each family, before we plan, how they want to make decisions and take part, and how the child will have a say. We follow their answer. The family chooses who takes part, where and when we meet, and what we leave out.

x: We will go through each draft plan with the family, against their family record, before it goes for sign-off. We sign off a plan, or a part of it, only when the family says it is theirs. t: We will treat the family's knowledge of their child as expert knowledge. We ask the family
x: We will treat the family's knowledge of their child as expert knowledge. We ask the family first, write their answers in their own words, and record both views when ours differ.

x: We will work out the family's strengths, needs and priorities with them, in conversation, before any plan is drafted. The family puts their priorities in their own order, and gets their copy within 5 business days of checking it with us.

t: We will fit each plan to how the child and each adult learn and live. We answer a request
x: We will fit each plan to how the child and each adult learn and live. We answer a request to change times, place, practitioner or way of working within 2 business days. We make the change by the date the family asks, or say why we cannot.

x: We will ask each family about their language, culture, beliefs and community before the plan is written and at every review. Where a family identifies as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander we offer to work alongside the community-controlled organisation they choose.

x: We will give information in the language, format and amount the family chooses. We check understanding by asking the family to say or show it back.

x: We will fit each strategy into a routine the family already has, and name that routine in the plan. We add a separate therapy time only if the family chooses it.

x: We will help each family build their own network of people, groups and services, as the family chooses. t: family: the parents, carers and other people who raise the child, as the family describes
x: family: the parents, carers and other people who raise the child, as the family describes itself. family-centred: working so that the family's knowledge, choices and priorities lead, and the family can change what we do. family record: the completed FRM-ECS-02 for one child. It holds what the family knows about their child, and their strengths. It also holds what is hard, what they want most, how they learn and live, and how they want to work with us. priority: something the family wants most for their child or their family, in the family's words and order. plan check: going through the draft plan with the family, against the family record, and asking whether the plan is theirs. plan lead: the practitioner accountable for the child's plan and the register row. key worker: the one practitioner the family chooses as their main contact. Where the family chooses a key worker, that person is the plan lead. practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners. routine: something the child and family do most days, such as meals, play, bath time or travel. network: the people, groups and services the family turns to for help, advice or a break. parental responsibility: the legal authority to make decisions for a child. A court or a child protection agency can change who holds it. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Start this procedure when: a family accepts our offer of early childhood supports (steps 1
w: Family-Centred Practice and Key Worker Procedure
x: Start this procedure when: a family accepts our offer of early childhood supports (steps 1 to 4) any practitioner has a contact with the family: a session, a call, a message or a meeting (steps 5 to 13) the family has chosen a key worker, has chosen none, or wants to change (steps 14 to 20) the family says no, asks for a change, sees something differently, or is unhappy (steps 21 to 24 and Decision table 1) a plan review is due (step 25). Who acts: The Service Manager names the plan lead and a backup. The plan lead opens the child's row, explains how we work, and is the family's first call where the family chose no key worker. The offer of a key worker and the family's choice are made under PRO-ECS-05 Collaboration Procedure (Early Childhood Supports). They are recorded in Section D of FRM-ECS-04 Team Around the Child Record. This procedure starts from that choice. t: Telling before asking makes the practitioner the only expert. The family's knowledge is lo
w: Family-Centred Practice and Key Worker Procedure
x: Telling before asking makes the practitioner the only expert. The family's knowledge is lost, and the family stops speaking up. Ask first. A strategy that does not fit the family's week will not be used. The family is blamed, and the child gets no benefit. Work inside their routines. "Do you understand?" gets a yes whatever the truth. The family leaves unsure what to do. Ask them to say or show it back. A family's no is a choice. Reducing a support because of a no punishes the child. It can breach the duty to respect self-determination and decision-making (Code of Conduct Rules, s 6(1)(a)). A child's safety comes before a family's choice. If you think a child may be at risk of harm, tell the child safety lead the same day. A delay can leave a child in danger. A child or a brother or sister who interprets can change what is said. The meaning is lost, and a child carries an adult's worries.

t: A plan written first and signed later is not the family's plan. The family stops taking pa
x: A plan written first and signed later is not the family's plan. The family stops taking part, and the plan misses what matters to them. A family can tell you something that means a child is at risk of harm. Stop and act the same day (step 5). A delay can leave a child unprotected. Culture, faith and beliefs are the family's to describe. A guess from a name, a look or a language is often wrong and breaks trust. Information about other adults belongs to them. Write only what the family chooses to tell you, in their words. A parent's health in a child's file can be shared by mistake. A gift, payment or benefit for a referral breaks the family's trust. It can breach the duty to act with integrity, honesty and transparency (Code of Conduct Rules, s 6(1)(d)). Law changing: from 20 November 2026 the NDIS Act bans inducements to provide supports.

x: assessment: the record, on FRM-ECS-03, of how a child functions in their everyday routines: what they do, with whom and with what help. It is made with the family. everyday routines: the things the child does most days, such as meals, play, bath time, getting dressed, travelling and going to early learning. everyday places: the places where the child's everyday life happens, such as home, early learning, school, playgroup, parks, shops and places of worship. These are the child's natural learning environments. taking part: the child doing something that matters to them and their family in a routine or place. It means joining in, choosing or helping, and not only being there. inclusion: the child taking part in the same routines as other children their age, in the same places. setting: an early learning service, school, playgroup or other group the child goes to. educator: a person who teaches or cares for the child in a setting, or leads the group. priority: a routine the family most wants the child to take part in more. link: a connection between the family and a community group, service or agency. support away from the child's everyday places: a support delivered in our rooms, or anywhere else where the child's routine does not happen. key worker: the one practitioner the family chooses as their main contact. Where the family chooses a key worker, that person is the plan lead. advocate: an independent person who helps a family speak up and be heard. We help the family find one. We do not choose for them. plan lead: the practitioner accountable for the child's plan and the register row. practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners. parental responsibility: the legal authority to make decisions for a child. A court or child protection order can change who holds it. trigger: an event, listed in Decision table 2 of PRO-ECS-04, that makes a review due before its date. family: the parents, carers and other people who raise the child, as the family itself describes them. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

x: Plan lead: give the family the summary within 5 business days of the last visit (step 24, our standard). Plan lead: sign the form. A young child often has several services in their life at once. This policy sets how [Prov
x: A young child often has several services in their life at once. This policy sets how [Provider name] works as one team with the family and those services. The family never has to carry messages between them.

t: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. Every practit
x: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. Every practitioner, key worker and manager of ours who works with those children. x: We will explain what a key worker is and ask every family whether they want one, within 10 business days of naming our plan lead. We ask again at every plan review and at least every 6 months.

x: Team around the child: the family, and every person or service that supports the child and that the family wants in the team. t: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us (the participant), and their fam
x: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us (the participant), and their family. t: coaching: helping a parent, carer, educator or other provider practise a strategy in the c
x: coaching: helping a parent, carer, educator or other provider practise a strategy in the child's own routine, in place of doing it for them. capacity building support: any support other than a coaching visit that builds the skill or knowledge of a person in the child's life. It can be a demonstration, a short training for educators, a picture guide or a shared video. support network: the relatives, friends, educators and providers in the child's everyday life whom the family chooses to involve. routine: something the child does most days, such as a meal, bath time, play, getting dressed, a trip, or group time at early learning. functional outcome: something the child will do in daily life, written in the plan so the family can see when it has happened. confidence rating: how confident a person says they feel, at the end of a session, to use the strategy for an outcome on their own this week, from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very). joint session: a session in which our practitioner and another provider work with the family together. sharing log: the list in FRM-ECS-04 Team Around the Child Record of every exchange of information outside the family. plan lead: the practitioner accountable for the child's plan and the register row. key worker: the one practitioner the family chooses as their main contact. Where the family chooses a key worker of ours, that person is the plan lead. practitioner: the worker of ours who runs a coaching session. Practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners, who gives each practitioner reflective supervision and reads their records. feedback review: a session in which the plan lead asks each person how useful the coaching is and how working together is going. child safety lead: the role the Chief Executive names to receive every concern about a child and to see that reports are made. reflective supervision: a meeting in which a practitioner and the Practice supervisor look at the practitioner's own work and learn from it. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Control
Capacity Building Procedure (Early Childhood Supports)
The result: each person in the child's life leaves every session more able and confident t
x: The result: each person in the child's life leaves every session more able and confident to help the child reach the plan's outcomes. The family comes first. What they tell us changes how we work. This procedure gives effect to POL-ECS-06 Capacity Building Policy (Early Childhood Supports), C1 to C13.

t: Start this procedure when the family agrees the interim plan under PRO-ECS-08 Outcome Base
x: Start this procedure when the family agrees the interim plan under PRO-ECS-08 Outcome Based Approach Procedure (Early Childhood Supports), within 10 business days of the first session, and again when the full plan, FRM-ECS-07 Child and Family Support Plan, is approved. Then follow it for every coaching session, joint session, capacity building support and feedback review. A session can be at home, at early learning, at school, in the community, at our premises or by phone or video. Who acts: The plan lead books the first session, enters sessions in the register and holds the feedback review. The plan lead also decides what to change and tells people (steps 1 and 24 to 27). The practitioner runs each session and records it (steps 2 to 23). The Practice supervisor reads session records and agrees one change with each practitioner (step 28). The Service Manager checks the register every month (step 29). The Quality Manager reads the feedback and ratings across all children every 6 months (step 30). In a small provider one person may hold several of these roles. A sole trader is the plan lead, the practitioner and the Service Manager. A sole trader engages one outside clinical supervisor with early childhood experience as the Practice supervisor, whose quarterly read covers coaching, practice and plans together. A sole trader also asks the independent contact named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register to read 3 session records every 6 months.

t: The family has agreed the interim plan, or the full plan is approved. You have read its ou
x: The family has agreed the interim plan, or the full plan is approved. You have read its outcomes and the routines it names. You have read the team record, FRM-ECS-04 Team Around the Child Record. You know who is in the team and what the family agreed may be shared. Your worker screening clearance and your working with children check are current in REG-HRM-01 Worker Screening Register. You have signed FRM-CHS-01 Child Safe Code of Conduct and Acknowledgement. You have the last FRM-ECS-05 Coaching Session Record for this child and the last note you gave. You have a blank FRM-ECS-05. It holds the confidence scale. You are trained to coach, and the training is recorded in REG-HRM-02 Training and Competency Register. An interpreter is booked if the family wants one. For a phone or video session, a parent, carer or educator is with the child.

t: A worker alone with a child. A worker out of sight of a parent, carer or educator puts the
x: A worker alone with a child. A worker out of sight of a parent, carer or educator puts the child at risk. It also exposes the worker to a false claim. Sharing without consent. Telling an educator or another provider about the child without the family's agreement breaks trust. It can also breach the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). Filming. A recording of a child, or of another child in the room, without written agreement is a privacy breach and a child safety risk. Taking over. If you do the strategy for the person every time, they do not learn it. The child's progress stops when you leave. Rating for the person. Your own view in the person's rating box hides what they told you. The register then shows progress that is not real. A strategy outside your scope. Coaching eating, drinking or swallowing without the qualified practitioner's written release, or medicine or any health procedure without the right qualification, can seriously hurt a child. A strategy that restrains a child. Coaching anyone to restrain, seclude or confine a child can cause harm and breach the child's rights. Challenge in public. Questioning a person's practice in front of the child, another family or their colleagues shames them and ends the working relationship. Feedback that is a complaint. A complaint left in a session record can sit unanswered. The person may stop telling us anything.

t: Evidence-Informed Practice Policy (Early Childhood Supports)
[Provider name] uses strategies that rest on stated principles and the best available evid
x: [Provider name] uses strategies that rest on stated principles and the best available evidence. Our practitioners choose strategies within their professional scope and with the family, write down what each one rests on, and keep their skills current. This policy is for families, our practitioners and the people who check our work.

t: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. Every strateg
x: Every child who receives early childhood supports from us, and their family. Every strategy we use or recommend: an approach, a programme, a technique, an assessment tool, an outcome measure or a piece of equipment. Every practitioner and manager of ours who delivers, plans or oversees early childhood supports. This covers employees, contractors, students and volunteers. Every setting: the family home, early learning, school, the community, our premises, and phone or video. A student or volunteer follows this policy with a practitioner watching. This policy does not bind other providers. It sets how we check what we use with them.

t: Commitments
We will use only strategies that rest on stated principles and the best available evidence
x: We will use only strategies that rest on stated principles and the best available evidence. A practitioner chooses a strategy within their professional scope. Before they first use it with a child, they make a short entry on FRM-ECS-06 Section C: the principle it rests on, one or two sources or the practice wisdom and family preference it draws on, any risk or legal limit, and who may deliver it. The Practice supervisor adds it to the one-page strategy list within 10 business days of the entry. A strategy is not held back while it is listed, unless it fails the restraint or law questions.

t: We will never bar a strategy only because it has no published evidence. Where the evidence
x: We will never bar a strategy only because it has no published evidence. Where the evidence is limited, the practitioner's reasoning and the family's preference may support its use as a monitored trial, with the outcome's measure in the child's plan and a look at the next progress check. We do not use a strategy shown to harm, or shown not to work for children like this one. We write the evidence basis in words, never as a letter grade.

t: We will not use a strategy that restrains, secludes or confines a child, or that breaks a
x: We will not use a strategy that restrains, secludes or confines a child, or that breaks a law that applies to it. Every evidence entry answers the restraint and law questions before the strategy is used.

t: We will have the Practice supervisor review the strategy list every 3 months. The Practice
x: We will have the Practice supervisor review the strategy list every 3 months. The Practice supervisor may ask for a change: another source, a limit, a measure, or that a strategy stops. We also review a strategy within 20 business days of learning of new evidence that could change its use. If new evidence shows a strategy may harm a child, we stop it the same day.

t: We will tell each family what the evidence says, in plain words and before they agree. We
x: We will tell each family what the evidence says, in plain words and before they agree. We say how sure we are, what the strategy asks of them and what else they could choose, and we record their decision on the child's plan. If a family asks for a strategy that is not on our list, the practitioner makes the entry the same way, and we give the family our answer within 20 business days.

t: We will check every handout, picture guide and video against the strategy entry before we
x: We will check every handout, picture guide and video against the strategy entry before we give it out, and again at the quarterly review of the list.

t: We will let a registered or certified practitioner deliver a strategy within their profess
x: We will let a registered or certified practitioner deliver a strategy within their professional scope without a separate sign-off. A per-practitioner sign-off, given after a qualified practitioner has watched at least 2 sessions, is needed only for a health-related strategy: eating, drinking, swallowing, medicine or a health procedure. A practitioner may deliver another discipline's strategy (role release) when the qualified practitioner has written on the strategy list what is released, has shown it, and reviews it at a set interval. Medicine and health procedures are never released.

t: We will give each practitioner the information and expertise to support the child and the
x: We will give each practitioner the information and expertise to support the child and the people in the child's life. Each can reach the National Best Practice Framework for Early Childhood Intervention (2025), the evidence for our strategies and a named expert to ask. If nobody we can reach has the expertise a child needs, we tell the family and refer or take advice.

t: We will give each practitioner reflective supervision with the Practice supervisor at leas
x: We will give each practitioner reflective supervision with the Practice supervisor at least every 3 months. Each one ends with one agreed change to practice.

t: We will have each practitioner assess their own practice against best practice within 60 b
x: We will have each practitioner assess their own practice against best practice within 60 business days of starting, and every 12 months. Every rating needs an example from a record; a new starter may use an example from a previous role, with no child's name. The Practice supervisor reviews it within 10 business days and agrees up to 3 goals.

t: We will arrange a peer review of each practitioner's practice at least every 6 months. The
x: We will arrange a peer review of each practitioner's practice at least every 6 months. The peer watches a session with the family's agreement, reads 2 session records or talks through a case with no names. The peer gives feedback within 5 business days. For a sole trader, a case discussion with the outside clinical supervisor is the peer review.

t: We will plan and record each practitioner's professional development. Each completes the h
x: We will plan and record each practitioner's professional development. Each completes the hours their professional standard sets (the Board's standard for a registered profession, Speech Pathology Australia's for speech pathology, the teacher registration body's for an early childhood teacher), and at least 20 hours in each 12 months, pro rata, where the profession sets none. At least half is on early childhood intervention practice. We count hours as the practitioner's professional standard counts them. We check within 3 months whether practice changed.

t: We will monitor our practice against what happens for children. Every 3 months the Practic
x: We will monitor our practice against what happens for children. Every 3 months the Practice supervisor's one quarterly read covers two plans of each practitioner against the strategy list and the outcomes, together with their session records under POL-ECS-06 Capacity Building Policy (Early Childhood Supports). Every 6 months the Quality Manager reports what the results show in the one early childhood quality report covering sections 56 to 62.

t: We will stop at once any use of a strategy that fails the restraint or law questions, and
x: We will stop at once any use of a strategy that fails the restraint or law questions, and any health-related practice outside a worker's qualification or sign-off. The Practice supervisor looks into each concern within 5 business days. Nobody is disadvantaged for raising a concern.

t: Ground rules
We weigh three things together: the best available research, the practitioner's skill, and
x: We weigh three things together: the best available research, the practitioner's skill, and what the child and family value and choose. None decides alone.

t: Every strategy follows six principles, drawn from the National Best Practice Framework for
x: Every strategy follows six principles, drawn from the National Best Practice Framework for Early Childhood Intervention (2025). Principle 1: the family leads. They know their child best and make the decisions. Principle 2: learning happens in everyday routines, in the places the child lives, learns and plays. Principle 3: we build the skills and confidence of the people around the child. Principle 4: we start from the strengths of the child and the family. Principle 5: we work as one team, with the family at the centre. Principle 6: the child's rights, voice and safety come first. A strategy that cannot follow principle 1 or 6 is never used.

t: A family can say no to any strategy, rating, recording or peer watching a session. Saying
x: A family can say no to any strategy, rating, recording or peer watching a session. Saying no never reduces supports.

t: No strategy of ours may restrain, seclude or confine a child, or limit what they can reach
x: No strategy of ours may restrain, seclude or confine a child, or limit what they can reach or use in order to change their behaviour. If a child's behaviour seems to need one, the Service Manager is told the same day and gets specialist behaviour support advice.

t: A health-related strategy (eating, drinking, swallowing, medicine or any health procedure)
x: A health-related strategy (eating, drinking, swallowing, medicine or any health procedure) is used only by a practitioner qualified and signed off for it. A mealtime or swallowing strategy may be coached by the key worker under role release, where the qualified practitioner's written plan names what is released, they have shown the key worker, and they review it at a set interval. Medicine and health procedures are never released. The child's plan names the qualified practitioner.

t: A source written, funded or sold by the maker or seller of a strategy needs a second sourc
x: A source written, funded or sold by the maker or seller of a strategy needs a second source with no link to them. A testimonial or a website alone is not a source.

t: A child's name never goes into a practice record, a peer review or a group learning sessio
x: A child's name never goes into a practice record, a peer review or a group learning session. We use the child's record number. We share a child's information only as the family's consent allows.

t: Reflection, self-assessment and peer review are for learning. A rating or a reflection is
x: Reflection, self-assessment and peer review are for learning. A rating or a reflection is never, by itself, a reason for discipline. We act at once if a record shows a child at risk, or work outside a qualification.

x: A concern about how a colleague practises goes to the Practice supervisor. t: strategy: any approach, programme, technique, assessment tool, outcome measure or piece of
x: strategy: any approach, programme, technique, assessment tool, outcome measure or piece of equipment that we use or recommend to a child or family. evidence entry: the short written entry for one strategy, in Section C of FRM-ECS-06. It covers the principle, the evidence basis, the risks, the legal limits, who may deliver it and the family summary. evidence basis: what a strategy rests on, written in words: a current framework or guideline; a review or study; limited or early evidence; or practice wisdom and the family's preference with no harm signal. A strategy shown to harm, or shown not to work for children like this one, has no basis and is not used. monitored trial: use of a strategy whose evidence basis is limited or rests on practice wisdom and family preference, with the family's agreement, the outcome's measure in the plan and a look at the next progress check. strategy list: the one-page list of every strategy we use, with its number, principle, evidence basis, who may deliver it, any limit or role release, and its last quarterly review. The Practice supervisor keeps it in the practice file until a Rise strategy register exists. family summary: what we tell a family about a strategy, in plain words. It covers what the strategy is, what it asks of them and what the evidence says. It also says how sure we are, what else they could choose, and any risk or cost. best practice framework: the National Best Practice Framework for Early Childhood Intervention (2025), or the later edition listed in REG-GOV-03. sign-off: the Practice supervisor's written confirmation that a practitioner may deliver a health-related strategy on their own. Other strategies need no sign-off; the practitioner's professional scope covers them. professional scope: what a practitioner's registration or certification and their training let them do. The practitioner and the Practice supervisor write its limits at FRM-ECS-06 question 3. role release: a qualified practitioner writing on the strategy list what part of their discipline's strategy another practitioner may deliver, showing them, and reviewing it at a set interval. health-related strategy: a strategy for eating, drinking, swallowing, medicine or any health procedure. practice record: FRM-ECS-06 for one practitioner for one practice year of 12 months. practice file: the place where the Practice supervisor keeps each practitioner's practice record and what supports it. self-assessment: a practitioner's own rating of their practice on eight domains, with an example from a record for each. reflective supervision: a meeting where a practitioner and the Practice supervisor look at the practitioner's own work and its evidence, and agree one change. peer review: a colleague with no authority over the practitioner watches a session, reads two session records or talks through a case, then gives feedback. professional development: learning that builds a practitioner's skills and knowledge, such as courses, reading with notes, mentoring and learning groups. Supervision and peer review time count only where the practitioner's professional standard counts them. practitioner: a worker of ours who delivers or plans early childhood supports. Practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners. In a small provider, one outside clinical supervisor with early childhood experience. plan lead: the practitioner accountable for the child's plan and the register row. key worker: the one practitioner the family chooses as their main contact. Where the family chooses a key worker of ours, that person is the plan lead. child safety lead: the role the Chief Executive names to receive every concern about a child and to see that reports are made. support network: the relatives, friends, educators and providers in the child's everyday life whom the family chooses to involve. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

t: Does the strategy restrain, seclude or confine the child, or limit what they can reach or
w: Practice Reflection and Professional Development Record
x: Does the strategy restrain, seclude or confine the child, or limit what they can reach or use in order to change their behaviour? The test is the primary purpose: is it done to manage or change the child's behaviour? Examples of a yes: holding a child still to stop a behaviour, shutting a child in a space, strapping a child to stop them moving, a medicine given to calm behaviour, locking away things or places to change behaviour. Not restraint: hand-over-hand prompting the child accepts, holding a hand to cross a road, a reflexive hold to stop a child running into danger, a high chair, car seat, cot or stair gate used for safety, or a medicine the child's doctor prescribes for a health condition (NDIS (Restrictive Practices and Behaviour Support) Rules 2018, section 6). A yes means stop: the strategy is not used, and you tell the Service Manager the same day. If you are not sure, answer yes and ask. Where a child already has an authorised behaviour support plan from another provider, we never coach its regulated practices; the behaviour support practitioner guides the family. A behaviour support practitioner confirms this wording at adoption. Choose one: no; yes. t: plan: the written plan for one child and their family. It holds the outcomes, the supports
w: Outcome Based Approach Policy (Early Childhood Supports)
x: plan: the written plan for one child and their family. It holds the outcomes, the supports, the measures and the review dates. FRM-ECS-07 is the plan. version: one dated copy of the plan. A new version is made when an outcome, a measure or a support changes. interim plan: version 0 of the plan, agreed with the family within 10 business days of the first session. It holds one to three starting outcomes and their supports, in the family's words, with no five-level scale. Coaching starts under it. The full plan replaces it. functional outcome: something the child or the family will do in daily life, written so anyone can see or hear when it has happened. priority: something the family wants most, in the family's own order and words, as recorded in FRM-ECS-02. need: something that is hard for the family right now, as recorded in FRM-ECS-02. support: what will be done in a routine to help an outcome happen. The Quality Indicators call it an intervention. routine: something the child does most days, such as a meal, bath time, play, a trip or group time at early learning. assessment: any way we look at what the child does and needs, to build the plan. It includes FRM-ECS-03, a practitioner's assessment and a standardised tool. starting point: where the child or family is now for an outcome, before work on it begins. five-level scale: five levels written with the family for one outcome. Level 3 is what the family hopes to see by the next plan review. progress check: a meeting with the family at least every 3 months, to agree the level of each outcome and to check each support. progress word: one of achieved, progressing, no change or gone back. We choose it at each progress check, using the rule at FRM-ECS-07 Q30. progress report: what we give the family to show how each outcome is going, in the format they chose. plan review: a meeting with the family, at least every 6 months, to decide what to keep, change, stop or add. mode of communication: how a person gets and gives information: speech, sign, pictures, writing, audio or video. plan lead: the practitioner accountable for the child's plan and the register row. key worker: the one practitioner the family chooses as their main contact. Where the family chooses a key worker of ours, that person is the plan lead. Practice supervisor: the clinical supervisor of the early childhood practitioners. family: the parents, carers and other people who raise the child, as the family describes itself. business day: a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives.

w: Outcome Based Approach Procedure (Early Childhood Supports)

Who acts: The plan lead writes the plan with the family and runs every check, report and review. Where the family chose a key worker of ours, that person is the plan lead. Where the plan lead asks a practitioner to draft a part, that practitioner is the practitioner drafting for the plan lead: they work with the family and the plan lead stays accountable. PRO-ECS-03 The Family Procedure (Early Childhood Supports) uses the same role. Every practitioner who works with the child tells the plan lead what they see, and records each session in FRM-ECS-05 Coaching Session Record. The Service Manager approves each version of the plan, and checks the register every month. The Quality Manager reads the results for all children every 6 months. In a small provider one person may hold several roles. A sole trader holds every role. At step 16 a sole trader checks their own plan against Decision table 2 and signs it. The independent contact named in REG-GOV-01 Delegations Register reads a sample of 3 plans every 6 months. A business day is a day other than a Saturday, a Sunday or a public holiday in the state or territory where the participant lives. In this procedure, T0 means the day the Service Manager signs the child's assessment under PRO-ECS-04 Inclusion Procedure (Early Childhood Supports), step 26. For a check or review, you have the last approved version, the last progress checks and the FRM-ECS-05 entries for the plan period. You have set aside time. Most families need more than one conversation. The family sets the pace.

t: A plan approved before the family says it is theirs is not their plan. The family may not
w: Outcome Based Approach Procedure (Early Childhood Supports)
x: A plan approved before the family says it is theirs is not their plan. The family may not use it, and the supports may aim at the wrong things. An outcome about our activity or a test score shows we were busy, not that the child's life changed. The family cannot tell whether things are better. A health strategy written by a worker who is not qualified can injure the child. Only the qualified practitioner writes it. A plan in words the family cannot read is not a copy they can use. They cannot hold us to it, and they may stop taking part. A report that is better than the truth hides a child who needs something different. It also breaches the duty to act with integrity, honesty and transparency (Code of Conduct Rules, s 6(1)(d)). A child, brother or sister who interprets can change what is said. Meaning is lost, and the child carries an adult's worries. A concern that a child is at risk of harm cannot wait for the plan. Act the same day (step 6). A delay can leave a child unprotected.
